Sports.title: Infantino to hold crisis meeting with senior FIFA staff
Sports.content:
Under-pressure FIFA president Gianni Infantino will hold a crisis meeting with senior staff in Morocco on Wednesday.

Senior staff have been asked to attend the meeting in Rabat after the pressure on the Swiss ramped up on Tuesday as:

Arsene Wenger and Infantino's number two criticised his plans to seek private investment in the World Cup

Jordan accused FIFA of "blackmailing" them over World Cup money in return for their support for Infantino

Ex-FIFA president Sepp Blatter backed Lise Klaveness to replace Infantino

Infantino is now set for crunch talks on Wednesday with senior FIFA staff after he was forced to withdraw his plan to create FIFA Forward Enterprise (FFE), a company to run the commercial and operational aspects of FIFA's tournaments.

Will Infantino resign at crisis meeting?

Sky Sports News' Kaveh Solhekol:



"This is going to be a very, very tense meeting. We don't know how it's going to end up.

"What is his stance going to be at this meeting? Is he going to throw in the towel and say, 'I can read the room. I can feel which way the wind is blowing. I'm losing support all over the world. I'm losing support inside FIFA as well. I'm going to do the honourable thing and resign.'

"Or is he going to say, 'I fight on. I'm the FIFA president. If you want me to leave, you're going to have to take me down. And I still believe that I have significant support around the world, especially in South America, Africa and Asia.'

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Sky Sports News takes a closer look at the controversies of Gianni Infantino's tenure at FIFA

"To get to the top of FIFA, you need to be a politician. And if you're a politician, surely you have some instincts. You can sense that you are losing support. You can sense that your position is untenable.

"You sense that you have to do the right thing and resign. Of course, it's going to be in terrible circumstances and he's going to resign in disgrace. If he does decide to resign, this is not the way he would have liked to go out.

"But he's made a cataclysmic error of judgment. And it was not just one quick decision that he got wrong. What we know is that he was plotting with some people close to him for quite a long time to sell off a stake in the World Cup to private investors.

"I haven't spoken to anybody who knows how FIFA works and how football politics works who thinks that Infantino can survive."

Wenger says FIFA U-turn 'necessary'

Former Arsenal manager Wenger, FIFA's chief of global football development, issued a statement on Tuesday saying he was "not involved" in the plan but that the decision to withdraw it was "absolutely necessary and beyond question".

Wenger had faced criticism in recent days for his silence over the FFE plans but spoke out on Tuesday to welcome the withdrawal of the project, adding: "I firmly believe in an independent FIFA that serves our game with commitment, transparency, and integrity."

Image: Arsene Wenger (left) with Infantino

FIFA secretary general Mattias Grafstrom, the second most senior figure in the organisation after Infantino, sent an email to FIFA staff addressing the "sad and reproachable series of events" of the last week "which thankfully concluded with the project being permanently abandoned".

Grafstrom also thanked FIFA staff for their efforts during the World Cup but accepted they had now been "thrown into the middle of a turmoil, which is difficult to comprehend and accept".

Grafstrom promised staff would be "defended and safeguarded from the political context we currently experience", pointedly adding: "Individuals, unstable moments and unfortunate episodes come and go. The institution, its mission and its responsibility towards world football continue."

The comments from Wenger and Grafstrom follow the resignation last week of Infantino's senior adviser Carlos Cordeiro, who described the FFE plan as a "bad deal for football".

Jordanian FA president accuses FIFA of 'blackmail'

Infantino's crisis deepened on Tuesday when FIFA were accused of "blackmailing" Jordan over World Cup money in return for their support for Infantino to stay on as president.

The support of national associations in Asia could prove critical to his survival, but the president of the Jordanian Football Association, Prince Ali Bin Al Hussein, wrote on X that his organisation "certainly" would not endorse Infantino after alleging FIFA sought to secure his support by promising it would help with the recovery of money he said was owed to the JFA.

Prince Ali, who stood for the FIFA presidency in 2015 against Sepp Blatter and against Infantino the following year, hit out at the difficulties faced by Jordanian fans seeking to enter the United States for this summer's World Cup and the "exorbitant" price of tickets, and detailed the "huge costs" in taxes his association faced due to being based in the US rather than Canada or Mexico for the finals.

He then revealed Jordan was still awaiting prize money from last year's Arab Cup, which is organised by FIFA, "while at the same time FIFA brags about how many billions they have in reserve".

"It is clear the problem really is with leadership," Prince Ali added.

"For months, FIFA has been refusing to help us on any of these or other matters - until it was verbally communicated to me during the World Cup that if I endorsed Infantino it would go a long way to helping our FA out.

"We pride ourselves in Jordan in upholding ethical values. We did not endorse him before and certainly will not now. But the whole situation amounts to blackmail and we refuse to give in to that."

Asia is seen as the key continent in any presidential contest that may yet be forced, with Europe and nations from North America, Central America and the Caribbean expected to want Infantino out while Africa, South America and Oceania are expected to back him.

UEFA has also told Infantino it is "actively considering" legal action over the FFE plan and lawyers acting on behalf of the European body have ordered Infantino and other FIFA staff to identify, locate and preserve any documents related to the project.

The plan to create FIFA Forward Enterprise (FFE), a company to run the commercial and operational aspects of FIFA's tournaments, first emerged in reports by The Times and The Financial Times last Tuesday, before FIFA issued confirmation of some of the details. The most controversial aspect of the plan was the idea to sell 20 per cent of FFE to private investors.

The plan was firmly rejected by European football's governing body UEFA, as well as CONCACAF - the confederation representing nations from North and Central America plus the Caribbean - and the Asian Football Confederation (AFC). UEFA also threatened to boycott FIFA competitions including the World Cup until the plan was scrapped, which it duly was last Saturday.

UEFA said it had nevertheless "lost confidence" in Infantino and a number of its associations - including those of England and Wales - have since formally withdrawn their support for Infantino, with the Scottish Football Association understood to be aligned to UEFA's position.

Blatter wants first female FIFA president to replace Infantino

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Sky Sports News' chief correspondent Kaveh Solhekol discusses the potential candidates who could challenge Infantino for the FIFA presidency

Former FIFA president Blatter says it is time for a woman to be FIFA president and he has backed Klaveness to replace Gianni Infantino.

Writing on his X account, Blatter says: "Lise Klaveness deserves the utmost respect. She was the only one who always took a clear stand and did not go along with the mainstream. And at FIFA, the time is right for a woman to take the lead".

Klaveness has been the president of the Norway Football Federation (NFF) for the past four years, and before that she was a lawyer and an international footballer.

Under her leadership, the NFF have taken a principled stand on a wide range of issues, even though it has meant being isolated and outnumbered by the vast majority of FAs who have meekly gone along with Infantino's schemes and plans.

She spoke out - in Qatar - about the World Cup being hosted in Qatar in 2022, and she has also criticised Saudi Arabia being awarded the 2034 World Cup in unusual circumstances.

The NFF were among only a handful of FIFA's 211 member associations that did not send letters earlier this year supporting Infantino's re-election bid in March 2027.

Blatter was FIFA president from 1998 to 2015 when he resigned in a corruption scandal.

He was cleared of personal corruption charges by a tribunal in Switzerland last August.

Sports.title: Why have Barcelona broken transfer records to sign Kerolin?
Sports.content:
It's been brief. Kerolin only joined the Women's Super League from the NWSL 18 months ago. She now leaves as the English top-flight's most expensive export.

Kerolin's £1.25m fee breaks record held by Olivia Smith's sale from Liverpool to Arsenal last summer. Barcelona were willing to smash their own transfer policy in pursuit of the Brazilian, too, having never previously paid a fee over £500k.

But Kerolin represents an exception to the rule. It's always been that way, from the start of her journey playing barefoot with boys on the streets of Sao Paulo. She was different. The ball hurt to kick, she confessed, but she did it anyway.

Image: Kerolin played a huge part in Man City winning their first WSL title for a decade in 2025-26

As such, there is perhaps an air of inevitability about the 26-year-old's switch to the four-time European champions. This is the path she expected to follow. "Always the most highly-ranked players are playing here or in Spain," she told Sky Sports upon signing for Man City in January 2025. "To be in the vision of the world."

She leaves a WSL champion.

Being considered among the game's most elite does not necessitate playing for Barcelona, but it helps. Each of the last five Ballon d'Or recipients were representing the Catalonia club at the time of winning the prize. Kerolin is now the team-mate of its current holder Aitana Bonmati.

Indeed, if Ballon d'Or is the mission Barcelona has proven the means. It's fertile ground for notoriety and success, with silverware almost guaranteed and the chance to star in a team undergoing reinvention under Pere Romeu. A summer of change has seen plenty of big names leave: Alexia Putellas, Ona Batlle and Mapi Leon among them.

Image: Former Barcelona captain Alexia Putellas is one of three players to join the WSL this summer

But the turning point for Kerolin follows the departure of forward Salma Paralluelo, a player similar in profile to her. The 22-year-old scored twice in last season's Champions League final, a precocious young talent with a huge appetite for success, now clubless after failing to agree terms.

Kerolin, who once held transfer interest from Arsenal, is perfectly poised to succeed her. Barcelona's need for a player of Kerolin's talents is greater than that of City's, flush with versatile wingers, while the considerable fee sends a well-timed message.

Maintenance as Europe's leading superpower does not come cheap. Barcelona have been burdened by financial constraints over the past few years, reliant on their global pull to attract and retain the game's top stars. But others have caught up; no longer is their lure enough in isolation.

To keep pace, Barcelona must show willing to be as financially front-footed as their European rivals. Kerolin's capture is a statement signing for a side in need of some validation after bidding farewell to four high-profile players in as many weeks. Proof that Romeu is remodelling, rather than revolutionising his team of aces.

Nor is this move an ego trip. Kerolin made 26 WSL appearances for Man City, scoring 12 goals. Only Khadija Shaw and Stina Blackstenius have a better goals-per-90 ratio during that time. No player can match Kerolin for take-ons attempted or completed.

In fact, very few forwards boast her complete skillset. She can balance scoring with creating, on-the-ball craft with off-the-ball industry, and has explosive speed in both directions. She scores screamers, too, with quality off both flanks.

Her departure less than two years after signing will feel premature for many in Manchester, not least City's leading scorer Shaw, for whom she made a habit of assisting.

But business is business; a rare deal where the benefits are mutually divided. Man City reap significant return on their investment and make space for one of their other wide forwards to make strides. Any one of Aoba Fujino, Mary Fowler, Iman Beney, or newly-recruited Beth Mead would fit the bill.

Barcelona, meanwhile, have a growing awareness of the increased competition they face to stay queens of Europe. They remain the highest benchmark for success for now, but need fresh impetus to stay there. Kerolin greatly enhances their chances.

Sports.title: Raducanu could benefit ending her season following US Open withdrawal
Sports.content:
Emma Raducanu could benefit from ending her season early to focus on recovery and secure a protected ranking before making her return in 2027, according to former British No 1 Annabel Croft.

The 23-year-old suffered a stress fracture to her right lower leg during the grass-court season and made a late decision to pull out of Wimbledon.

And following consultation with her medical team, Raducanu on Monday concluded she will be unable to play at the US Open later this month - live on Sky Sports.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player The US Open is live on Sky Sports Tennis this month

What is a Protected Ranking?

It is a provision in tennis that enables players who have been absent from the sport for an extended period to qualify more easily for tournaments upon their return.



The ATP and WTA Tours have different rules when it comes to protected rankings.



For ATP Tour or other men's tournaments, an eligible player could use a protected ranking calculated over the three months after they suffered an injury.



WTA Tour players see their protected rankings fixed as the same as it was at the time when the injury was first suffered.



A WTA player can use this protected ranking for eight tournaments in a year, or 12 if they miss more than a year.



Raducanu has only recently taken her first tentative steps back on court while wearing a protective boot, and the latest setback is another blow for the Brit after a frustrating 12 months plagued by persistent physical issues.

Speaking on Sky Sports Tennis, former player-turned-TV analyst Croft admitted "she's been unbelievably unlucky with injury problems."

"There are so many injuries out there but it seems like she never gets a clear run where she's able to really go for it with her tennis and her body and her mind and everything injury free and just keep the momentum going."

She finally returned for the end of the clay-court season having rehired Andrew Richardson, the coach who guided her to the US Open title, but the pair's time on court together has been limited.

Raducanu enjoyed one of the best weeks of her career by reaching her biggest final since New York at Queen's Club in June but it was that effort that triggered her latest setback.

She was not among the players named in Great Britain's team for the Billie Jean King Cup Finals in late September.

"I've seen lots of pictures of her posting with the boot on her leg and just trying to serve, to keep her racket going and showing everybody that she's doing everything she can. But clearly, it's not healed up," said Croft, who retired from the professional tour at the age of 21.

A protected ranking for Raducanu?

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Take a look back at Emma Raducanu's incredible win at the 2021 US Open. The tournament is live on Sky Sports Tennis this month

There will now be question marks over whether Raducanu, who will slide from her current ranking of 49, will compete again in 2026 with the temptation of a protected ranking.

Should she miss at least six months of competition due to injury, she can use a special ranking for a select number of events upon her return. This would be her top-50 ranking from during the grass season - the last time she competed and received prize money for a tournament.

Raducanu is at the risk of dropping down the rankings with a lot of points to defend following last year's north American hard-court swing in Washington, Canada, Cincinnati, and the US Open.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Both Tim Henman and Laura Robson believe Raducanu reuniting with her former coach is a good move

"It wouldn't be a surprise if she made that decision [close down her season]," said Croft, a former world No 24. "That wouldn't be such a bad decision to take because you can fully heal, rest up, get as much treatment as possible and then come out fully fit, raring to go at the start of next year.

"Maybe if there's a worry about the ranking drop with so many points to defend and potentially that ranking could plummet, although she might benefit from the protected ranking.

"All of these factors have to be considered, don't they? But at the end of the day, your health is your wealth, as they say, and that is the most important factor and she just needs to get herself fit.

"It's an unusual injury. I mean, I've had calf muscle injuries, which were not nice at all. And the minute you push off, you tweak it and it feels tight but the one thing that I've always thought about Raducanu, particularly when we saw her at Queen's Club on the grass where she played such beautiful tennis, is that she's very light on her feet. Movement has always been one of her strengths.

"She's such a great athlete. She moves around the ball. She's light on her feet and gets into great positions where she never looks off balance. But movement will be part of a major strength of what she brings out onto the court. That needs to be absolutely 100 per cent."

Sports.title: McKenna to target Eubank Jr and more after dream world title fight
Sports.content:
Aaron McKenna believes winning the middleweight title will pave the way for fights against some of the biggest names in boxing.

Ireland's McKenna gets his dream world title fight on Saturday, live on Sky Sports, when he boxes Etinosa Oliha for the IBF championship at the 3Arena in Dublin.

"It's something I've been dreaming of since I started boxing at six years old. Finally to get a fight for the world title and for it to be in Ireland makes it extra special," McKenna told Sky Sports.

"I have goosebumps just thinking about fighting in there with that Irish atmosphere.

"20 years I've been boxing and it's all going to come down to this night."

McKenna believes victory would put him in the frame for more high profile fights.

Sports.title: Fifa accused of using ‘blackmail’ to force support for Infantino’s re-election bid
Sports.content:
The Jordan Football Association president, Prince Ali bin al-Hussein, has accused Gianni Infantino’s administration of “blackmail”, claiming that Fifa threatened to withhold financial assistance from his federation if it refused to back the president’s bid for re-election.

In a major intervention Prince Ali, who ran for the Fifa presidency against Infantino in 2016 and finished third, listed a number of problems dogging the global governing body and said Jordan’s players have not yet been paid for appearing in the Arab Cup last year. Prince Ali is head of the West Asian Football Federation, which includes influential states such as Qatar and the United Arab Emirates that have thus far backed Infantino to stay on.

It came on a day when Infantino’s authority was dealt a further blow as two more key allies distanced themselves from his failed World Cup private investment plan. His No 2, the Fifa secretary general, Mattias Grafström, was revealed to have called the botched Fifa Forward Enterprise a “sad and reproachable series of events” in an email to the organisation’s staff. Meanwhile the former Arsenal manager Arsène Wenger, who is now Fifa’s chief of global development, said the project’s withdrawal was “absolutely necessary and beyond question”.

Infantino is steadily losing backing from countries who previously had sent letters to endorse his continuation for a fourth term in charge. It is understood that Greece is the latest federation to have pulled its support, following the lead taken by countries such as England, Wales, Finland and Serbia. More European federations are expected to follow in the coming days, while a number of nations in Concacaf – the North and Central American and Caribbean confederation – are also giving serious consideration to withdrawing their backing.

Prince Ali’s statement, published on X, painted the picture of a small country facing a litany of roadblocks when it came to receiving help from the global governing body. Jordan competed in their first World Cup this year but he explained some of their fans had not received visas, despite purchasing tickets, and expressed anger at being taxed by the US for being based in the country.

“We have been waiting for reward money for our players since December for the Arab Cup in Qatar, which is a Fifa event,” his statement read. “The money our team should receive for having reached the final has not been delivered yet, while at the same time Fifa brags about how many billions they have in reserve.

View image in fullscreen The Fifa president, Gianni Infantino (centre), and secretary general, Mattias Grafström (right), with Arsène Wenger during the 2026 World Cup. Photograph: ANP/Shutterstock

“It is clear the problem really is with leadership. For months, Fifa has been refusing to help us on any of these or other matters – until it was verbally communicated to me during the World Cup that if I endorsed Infantino it would go a long way to helping our FA out.

“We pride ourselves in Jordan in upholding ethical values. We did not endorse him before and certainly will not now. But the whole situation amounts to blackmail and we refuse to give in to that.”

Other countries are understood to have been put under concerted pressure to formally back Infantino before the Fifa election in March, although details of how it was applied remain unclear in those cases.

Grafstrom’s email had urged Fifa staff to keep morale high after what was perceived to be a successful World Cup. His message stopped short of criticising Infantino by name and promised to shield colleagues from the strife enveloping their organisation.

“A sad and reproachable series of events – which were thankfully concluded with the FFE project permanently abandoned – for as much as we feel dismayed by them, should not overshadow this reality,” read a section of the email.

11:54 Is Gianni Infantino’s time up as Fifa president? - The Latest

He referred to “a turmoil, which is difficult to comprehend and accept” and said: “Individuals, unstable moments and unfortunate episodes come and go. The institution, its mission and its responsibility towards world football continue, and that is why we should always keep our professionalism, sense of perspective and composure.”

Wenger, who assumed his current position in November 2019, confirmed he had been among the many senior Fifa staff sidelined by Infantino’s plan. “I was not involved in this strategic plan and first became aware of the project through media reports,” he said.

“The decision to withdraw the project was absolutely necessary and beyond question, because I firmly believe in an independent Fifa that serves our game with commitment, transparency, and integrity.”

Fifa was contacted for comment regarding Prince Ali’s accusations.

According to reports, Infantino has called Fifa staff to a crisis meeting in the Moroccan capital, Rabat, today as he tries to cling to his position.

Sports.title: Manchester United set to appoint former Hearts manager Eva Olid as new head coach
Sports.content:
Manchester United are set to appoint the former Hearts manager Eva Olid as their new head coach to replace Marc Skinner, following his exit on Monday, multiple sources have told the Guardian.

Talks with the 40-year-old are understood to be very advanced and she is expected to be introduced to the United squad on Wednesday.

United are confident that the Spanish coach is the right person to lead them into a new chapter, as first reported by the Telegraph, as the Women’s Super League club focuses on developing young, homegrown players.

Olid led Hearts to their first Scottish Women’s Premier League title last term on a dramatic final day of the season, but it had already been confirmed in April that she was to leave the Edinburgh club this summer by mutual agreement. She was in charge of Hearts for five years and also guided them to the 2024 Scottish Cup final, where they were beaten by Rangers.

She has previously coached in the United States with Houston Dynamo, working with their women’s team and their under-19s men’s squad, before she had a spell with the Catalan Football Association.

United are understood to be impressed by her playing style and her ability to develop and improve players, and they carried out extensive background checks on Olid prior to publicly announcing Skinner’s departure on Monday, with succession planning having already been well under way.

Skinner left partly because of frustration at United’s transfer strategy. The club are understood to feel the current level of spending across the WSL is unsustainable and they want a different approach, focusing on their own younger talents and improving their academy to deliver longer-term success.

View image in fullscreen Marc Skinner left Manchester United party because of frustration over the club’s transfer strategy. Photograph: John Clifton/Action Images/Reuters

United finished fourth in the WSL last term. They start the new season away to big-spending London City Lionesses on 4 September.

The news comes on the day that the United captain, Maya Le Tissier, said her team will “stick together” and be ready for the new WSL season, despite Skinner departing.

Le Tissier and the rest of the playing squad were informed by Skinner that he would be leaving, in a meeting on Monday morning shortly before the news was announced, and on Tuesday Le Tissier and her England teammate Ella Toone paid tribute to Skinner for his contribution to the club over five years in charge, which included winning the 2024 Women’s FA Cup.

Le Tissier said the “energy he brought to the club was amazing”, while Toone told reporters: “He wanted to tell the team before it came out. It was nice that he was able to tell us [and] he was able to say goodbye, because he’s done a lot for the club. We can’t thank him enough for everything he’s done, the hard work and the passion that he’s put into leading this team.”

Le Tissier said that neither she nor Toone have been consulted on who the next head coach should be but added: “I think the club have been pretty clear with what they’ve said, bringing through the youth, that’s what something Manchester United has been kind of made for, and they’ve always done that historically. I think they’ve been pretty clear with that. When we speak to the new manager, the ambitions will be clear.

“Me and Tooney are at Man United because we want to win and we’ll be doing everything we can to make that happen. We’ve got a great team, a great squad, great girls. I’m ready to do that.

“No matter who comes and goes, we’ve always had that togetherness and that fight for each other and we stick together in tough moments. There’s been a few over the years and we’ve always come through as a team, and, yeah, this one might be difficult right now, we’re in the start of pre-season and we want to make sure that we’re 100% ready for the start of the season.

“We spoke to the girls today, we’ll stick together, we always do. We’ve got to go out on the pitch, enjoy playing football and being with each other and we’ll get through it.”

Sports.title: Football Daily | Chelsea, Jordan Henderson and a transfer pivot for the ages
Sports.content:
A BRIDGE TOO FAR?

Who’s next? Can they convince Craig Gordon to reverse his recent retirement? Invite Bolo Zenden back for a second spell at Stamford Bridge? Get Kieran Richardson to replace Marc Cucurella? Chelsea really have cooked up a fascinating transfer policy: to recreate the Sunderland XI that triumphed 3-0 at the Bridge in November 2010. Danny Welbeck, 19 and on loan from Manchester United, sealed victory that day; Jordan Henderson, 20 and days away from his England debut, ran things in the middle alongside Lee Cattermole. Sixteen years later, Welbeck and Henderson are teammates once again, brought together by Chelsea’s sudden realisation that Alan Hansen had a point.

Henderson continues to surprise with his post-Liverpool career path, swapping Dammam for Amsterdam before exploring the different corners of west London, all in the space of three years. How can one say no to the charms of Xabi Alonso? “Given the size of the club, the manager, who I have great admiration for, and the quality of the ⁠players, this was a huge opportunity I couldn’t turn down,” Henderson bellowed, before awarding BlueCo a medal for participation. “I was also so impressed with how much the ownership want Chelsea to be successful and move in the right direction.”

It’ll take some time getting used to Henderson in blue, though you wonder just how much we’ll see of him on the pitch, his reputation nowadays less focused on what he does with the ball at his feet. Now it’s all about his role as The Standard Setter, the peace lily that brings a dressing room together. “The best guy I’ve ever come across I think in football,” cooed Morgan Rogers while on duty for England this summer, a view also taken by Jude Bellingham. Chelsea’s new record signing will surely welcome the soothing instructions of Hendo at Cobham.

The club’s pivot in transfer strategy is, of course, incredibly amusing: spending gargantuan sums on young talent before clocking on to the grand idea that not all of your first-team players should be eligible for a railcard. And even then, old habits die hard: the signing of Welbeck is yet another from Brighton, following the same path taken in recent seasons by Cucurella, Moisés Caicedo, Robert Sánchez and João Pedro. It all makes for a spectacular act of plagiarism, with Alonso’s Chelsea combining the Tony Bloom project down south with a flavour of Steve Bruce’s Sunderland. Football Daily looks forward to reading about Nedum Onuoha in Wednesday’s Rumour Mill.

QUOTE OF THE DAY

“I was not involved in this strategic plan and first became aware of the project through media reports. The decision to withdraw the project was absolutely necessary and beyond question, because I firmly believe in an independent Fifa that serves our game with commitment, transparency, and integrity” – Arsène Wenger, these days Fifa’s chief of global development, puts a metaphorical moat between himself and his president, Gianni Infantino. Fifa secretary general Mattias Grafström, Infantino’s No 2, has also called the failed World Cup private investment plan a “sad and reproachable series of events”.

View image in fullscreen Gianni Infantino watches the World Cup semi-final match between England and Argentina, flanked by Arsène Wenger (left) and Mattias Grafström (right). Photograph: ANP/Shutterstock

RECOMMENDED FOLLOWING

Big Website: on BlueSpace, TikBook, Instachat, you name it.

“Whoever wrote the Uefa statements over the weekend deserves a pay rise. Crystal clear messages, each line dripping with contempt and – for once – speaking for millions of football fans. ‘Thou shalt not pass’ at its best” – Gabriele Weber.

“The sublime Marcus Stewart scored for Huddersfield at Wolverhampton in September 1999, the game’s only goal, with a Panenka. Steve Bruce, his manager, said that, if he ever tried to do that again, he’d chip him. He took the warning seriously and didn’t try another even after Bruce left the club. Please give this a little space in your diary; not for my sake, but for Marcus’s, as he contends with the most appalling illness” – Richard Askham.

“Has anyone ever seen Infantino and The Hood from Thunderbirds in the same room?” – Craig Fawcett.

If you have any, please send letters to the.boss@theguardian.com. Today’s prizeless letter o’ the day goes to … Gabriele Weber. Terms and conditions for our competitions, when we run them, are here.

Sports.title: Barcelona sign Brazil forward Kerolin from Manchester City for club-record £1.25m
Sports.content:
Barcelona have signed the Brazil forward Kerolin from Manchester City for an undisclosed fee that sources say is in the region of £1.25m, which would represent the largest sum received for a sale by a Women’s Super League side.

The deal is also a club-record for Barcelona, and in terms of a fee received by an English club it eclipses the £1m that Liverpool received for the sale of Olivia Smith in Arsenal in 2025 and Melvine Malard’s more recent £850,000 switch from Manchester United to Chelsea.

Kerolin, 26, was part of the City side that won the WSL title and the Women’s FA Cup last season and was with the club for 18 months, after arriving from North Carolina Courage in January 2025.

City have already added the England forward Beth Mead to their squad this summer, on a free transfer from Arsenal.

The defending European champions Barcelona are understood to see Kerolin as a player who can thrive in the Champions League and become a regular goalscorer in that competition with her pace and trickery on the ball.

A statement from Barcelona, who said goodbye to the Spain internationals Alexia Putellas, Mapi León, Ona Batlle and Salma Paralluelo this summer, read: “The signing of Kerolin Nicoli is another clear statement of FC Barcelona’s ambition. The club remains committed to bringing together the best players in world football with the aim of staying at the top of the game and continuing to set the standard for excellence.
