According to the latest World Investment Report released by UN Trade and Development (UNCTAD), Kazakhstan accounted for nearly 66% of Central Asia’s total, solidifying its position as the region’s largest destination for foreign investment. The nation’s FDI stock, which refers to the accumulated value of FDI held in a country, stood at $156.4 billion as of 2025.

Kazakhstan’s improved position in the May 2026 update also reflects a broader shift in how investors assess emerging markets. For decades, lower labor and production costs were often enough to attract factories and integrate developing countries into global supply chains. That model is now weakening as capital increasingly targets digital infrastructure, advanced manufacturing and other complex industries.

This places greater weight on the country’s domestic capacity. Kazakhstan has been positioning itself for that shift by investing in transport corridors, energy infrastructure, digital connectivity and advanced manufacturing, accompanied by comprehensive support to investors.

World.title: Kazakhstan Releases First Tiger Into Wild in More Than 70 Years
World.content:
ASTANA — Kazakhstan has released a tiger into the wild for the first time in more than 70 years, marking a historic milestone in a decade-long effort to restore the predator to its former habitat and revive the wider ecosystem of the southern Lake Balkhash region.

An adult female Amur tiger named Umit, meaning “hope” in Kazakh, was released on July 31 in the Ile-Balkhash State Nature Reserve in southeastern Kazakhstan. Equipped with a satellite tracking collar, she is now moving independently through an area once inhabited by the extinct Caspian, or Turan tiger, reported the Ministry of Ecology and Natural Resources.

The release represents the first practical stage of Kazakhstan’s tiger reintroduction program and one of the country’s most ambitious wildlife restoration projects.

“Today, we witnessed a truly historic event,” Minister of Ecology and Natural Resources Yerlan Nyssanbayev said at the release ceremony.

“For the first time since the tiger disappeared from Kazakhstan more than 70 years ago, the first tiger has been released into its historical range. This is the result of many years of work by the state, our Russian colleagues, scientists and international partners,” he said.

Nyssanbayev said that the release was only the beginning of a much longer process.

“A great deal of work lies ahead to monitor the tigers and establish a sustainable population, but today we have taken the first and very important step,” he said.

“The tiger disappeared from Kazakhstan in 1948, and I would suggest that when Vsevolod Sysoyev signed the world’s first outright ban on tiger hunting in the Khabarovsk region that same year, he was guided in part by this evidence,” said Konstantin Chuychenko, Russia’s justice minister and chair of the supervisory board of the Amur Tiger Center.

“Awareness of the immediate threat of extinction, followed by enormous conservation efforts, made it possible to save the Amur tiger. Nearly 80 years later, animals from the Khabarovsk region are now helping restore the tiger population in Kazakhstan. This historical parallel underscores the depth and significance of cooperation between Russia and Kazakhstan,” he said.

A decade-long effort

The tiger stands at the top of the food chain. Its presence depends on healthy forests, reliable water resources, sufficient populations of wild ungulates and effective protection against poaching. Returning a tiger, therefore, required Kazakhstan to prepare an ecosystem and restore much of the natural ecosystem that once supported it. That preparation took more than 10 years.

The government established the Ile-Balkhash State Nature Reserve in 2018, strengthened protection of the territory, and worked to increase populations of wild boar, Bukhara deer and other animals that form the tiger’s natural prey base.

Adaptation enclosures, veterinary facilities and monitoring infrastructure were also constructed inside the reserve. Specialists were trained to track the animals, assess their behavior and respond to possible encounters between tigers and people.

How did tigers vanish?

The lower reaches of the Ili River and the southern Lake Balkhash area were once part of the natural range of the tiger. The predator inhabited the dense tugai forests and river floodplains of Central Asia, including areas along the Ili and Syr Darya rivers. These landscapes provided water, cover and abundant prey.

By the middle of the 20th century, however, the tiger had disappeared from Kazakhstan. The destruction and fragmentation of tugai forests, decline in the numbers of wild ungulates, expanding human activity and uncontrolled hunting left the predator without enough habitat or food to survive. The last reliably documented sightings in Kazakhstan occurred more than seven decades ago.

Four tigers bring hope

Umit, which translates as hope in Kazakh and gives the project a symbolic dimension, is one of the four tigers brought from Russia to Kazakhstan in May. The group includes an adult male named Amur, Umit and two cubs named Turan and Ussuri. The animals were brought from Russia’s Khabarovsk region and placed in specially constructed adaptation enclosures in the Ile-Balkhash reserve.

Before her release, Umit passed veterinary examinations and behavioral assessments aimed at determining whether she could live independently. Specialists evaluated her health, hunting ability, reaction to people and capacity to adapt to unfamiliar surroundings. The results indicated that she was ready to enter the wild.

Immediately before the enclosure was opened, Umit was fitted with a GPS/GSM satellite collar.

Her location and movements are now being monitored around the clock. Specialists are using satellite data, camera traps and field observations to study how she navigates the territory, selects resting sites and searches for prey.

The monitoring system is also designed to provide an early warning if the tiger approaches settlements or other areas of human activity.

Unlike males, which tend to travel considerable distances, females generally remain closer to their established territory. Releasing her first will allow specialists to observe her behavior at a stage when neither people nor the tigers themselves yet know what to expect.

Gradual approach

The adult male Amur remains in an enclosure and continues to undergo behavioral tests. A decision on his release will be made only after specialists conclude that he is prepared to survive independently.

The two cubs, which arrived in Kazakhstan at approximately six to seven months old, will remain under supervision as they grow and develop. The ministry said they are expected to stay in the reserve’s specialized enclosures until they are at least 18 months old. Each cub will then undergo separate veterinary and behavioral assessments before any decision is made about a possible release.

The gradual approach reflects the complexity of reintroducing a major predator.

The choice of the Amur tiger is rooted in science. In 2009, genetic research showed that the extinct Turan tiger and the Amur tiger are virtually identical, paving the way for plans to restore the species in Central Asia. Early signs suggest the animals can adapt.

Kazakhstan has moved beyond commemorating an animal that vanished from its territory and has begun the far more difficult task of creating a landscape in which that animal can live again. The long-term goal is to establish a viable, reproducing tiger population in the Ili River delta and the southern Lake Balkhash region.

Cooperation across borders

The program has been developed through cooperation between Kazakhstan and Russia, with support from scientists and international conservation organizations.

The two countries signed a memorandum on tiger reintroduction at the International Tiger Conservation Forum in Vladivostok in 2022. A joint working group was established to oversee the implementation of the tiger reintroduction program.

In February 2025, the working group held its first meeting in Kazakhstan. Russian experts inspected the Ile-Balkhash State Nature Reserve, and reviewed the infrastructure prepared for the arrival and adaptation of the animals. The second meeting took place in Khabarovsk in September 2025.

During President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev’s state visit to Russia in November 2025, the two countries signed a joint action plan for the transfer and adaptation of Amur tigers in Kazakhstan.

Under the approved plan, Kazakh specialists completed training in Russia in December 2025 and February 2026. The initiative has been described by its organizers as the first international program of its kind aimed at restoring a tiger population in a country where the animal had disappeared.

World.title: Why is Hydropower Becoming Central to Kazakhstan’s Clean Energy Strategy?
World.content:
ALMATY – Kazakhstan’s renewable energy strategy is entering a new phase. After a decade of rapidly expanding wind and solar generation, the government is shifting its focus to hydropower as the missing link needed to stabilize an increasingly renewable electricity system.

The shift became clearer on July 31, when the government approved a Hydropower Development Plan through 2035, creating the country’s first long-term framework for identifying new projects, mapping river basins and preparing investment-ready sites. The plan comes as Kazakhstan seeks to diversify its electricity mix while improving grid reliability, an increasingly important challenge as renewable energy capacity grows.

From renewable expansion to system stability

Kazakhstan’s renewable energy policy has produced measurable progress. Renewables generated 6.43% of the country’s electricity in 2024, exceeding the national 2025 target a year early. Installed renewable capacity reached 3.03 gigawatts, including 1.52 GW of wind, 1.22 GW of solar, and 287.7 MW of small hydropower.

At the same time, success has exposed a structural weakness familiar to electricity systems worldwide. Unlike conventional thermal power plants, wind turbines and solar panels generate electricity only when weather conditions allow. As their share in the grid increases, so does the need for flexible generation capable of balancing fluctuations in supply and demand.

This appears to be the problem Kazakhstan is now trying to address. The Hydropower Development Plan outlines 30 measures across six priority areas, including river basin assessments, hydrological studies, environmental evaluations, land preparation and the creation of a national database of potential hydropower sites.

A digital platform will consolidate hydrological, technical and environmental information into a single resource for government agencies and investors. Future project selection will consider water availability, electricity demand, technical feasibility, environmental constraints and investment potential.

Perhaps most importantly, the strategy also introduces planning for pumped-storage hydropower: facilities capable of storing excess electricity generated during periods of low demand and releasing it when consumption peaks, a technology widely regarded as one of the most effective ways of balancing renewable-heavy power systems.

Hydropower moves from supporting role

Although hydropower has long existed within Kazakhstan’s electricity mix, it has remained a relatively modest contributor compared with coal-fired generation and, more recently, wind and solar. The new plan elevates the sector’s role as it targets the commissioning of at least 500 megawatts of new hydropower capacity by 2030, while establishing a longer-term pipeline of conventional hydroelectric plants and storage facilities extending to 2035.

Several projects are already progressing, such as a 16-megawatt hydropower plant on the Kalzhyr River in East Kazakhstan, which is expected to be completed by 2030. Documentation is also underway for a 191.7 billion tenge (US$377.4 million) public-private partnership on the Ugam River that combines a drinking water pipeline with a cascade of hydroelectric stations. The project is expected to supply 110 million cubic meters of drinking water annually while generating 72 megawatt-hours of electricity.

Five larger hydropower stations in East Kazakhstan and the Zhetysu Region with combined capacity exceeding 1,000 megawatts are also being considered for strategic infrastructure status, while authorities have identified 29 hydraulic structures suitable for future small hydropower development.

Taken together, these projects illustrate that the strategy extends beyond individual power plants toward building an integrated hydropower portfolio.

A broader low-carbon strategy

The renewed focus on hydropower does not signal a retreat from wind and solar. Energy Minister Yerlan Akkenzhenov has reaffirmed Kazakhstan’s broader objective of commissioning 8.4 gigawatts of renewable energy capacity by 2035 as part of the country’s low-carbon development strategy at the Baku Energy Week this June.

Instead, the government’s latest plan reflects a subtle but important shift in thinking. The first phase of Kazakhstan’s energy transition centered on increasing renewable generation. The next phase appears to focus on ensuring the electricity system can accommodate that growth without compromising reliability.

As Ainur Sospanova, chairwoman of the Qazaq Green Renewable Energy Association, previously told The Astana Times, the rapid deployment of renewable energy is beginning to expose weaknesses within Kazakhstan’s electricity system. The challenge now is no longer simply adding renewable capacity, but developing the infrastructure necessary to integrate it. Hydropower, particularly pumped-storage facilities, could become one of the principal technologies providing that flexibility.

What comes next

Approving a long-term strategy, however, is only the first step. Hydropower projects typically require years of environmental assessments, hydrological studies, engineering work and financing negotiations before construction begins. Water availability, particularly in transboundary river basins, will remain a critical factor as climate variability places additional pressure on regional water resources.

For that reason, the success of the new strategy will likely be measured less by the number of plans approved than by whether Kazakhstan can convert them into viable projects. The indicators worth following over the coming years include the completion of the national hydrological database, the launch of bankable investment projects, the attraction of private capital and, perhaps most significantly, progress toward Kazakhstan’s first large-scale pumped-storage hydropower facility.

If those milestones are achieved, hydropower could become the technology that enables Kazakhstan’s next stage of decarbonization, transforming renewable expansion from a question of generation capacity into one of long-term system resilience.

World.title: Hosting Global AI Olympiad, Kazakhstan Looks Beyond Competition
World.content:
ALMATY – As more than 500 high school students from 106 countries gathered in Astana for the International Olympiad in Artificial Intelligence (IOAI), President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev used the event to showcase Kazakhstan’s broader ambition to become one of Eurasia’s leading AI economies. But while hosting global competitions highlights the country’s growing digital profile, experts say long-term success will depend less on attracting talent than on creating an ecosystem capable of retaining it, commercializing research and translating education into innovation.

Speaking at the opening ceremony of the Olympiad, which runs from Aug. 2 to 8, Tokayev described artificial intelligence as one of the central pillars of Kazakhstan’s long-term development strategy.

President Tokayev also said that Kazakhstan has made a “strategic choice” in favor of digital transformation, pointing to the country’s ranking of 24th in the United Nations E-Government Development Index and its position as Central Asia’s leader in technological readiness.

“We are creating a unified innovative ecosystem in which artificial intelligence serves as an important tool for managing the state, economy, and business, permeating all areas of public life,” Tokayev said.

AI is indeed becoming an essential tool for government, business and public services as Kazakhstan works toward becoming a fully digital state within three years. The designation of 2026 as the Year of Digitalization and Artificial Intelligence and the inclusion of innovation in the country’s new Constitution are intended to accelerate that transition.

The IOAI, however, reflects a broader objective than technological modernization alone. As one of the newest international science olympiads, established in 2024, the competition seeks not only to identify talented students but also to create an international community of future AI researchers while encouraging discussion about the opportunities and ethical challenges posed by artificial intelligence.

Kazakhstan was among the founding members of the Olympiad and became the first Central Asian country to host the event.

Building an AI pipeline

The country’s AI strategy increasingly spans the entire talent pipeline from schools to research infrastructure and commercial applications. Last year, Kazakhstan’s team won three gold, one silver and three bronze medals at the Olympiad in Beijing, a result Tokayev said demonstrated the country’s growing pool of young scientific talent.

Kazakhstan’s Competitive Programming Federation President Bagdat Mussin argued that such achievements should complement rather than replace higher education.

“Computer science, programming and artificial intelligence are becoming essential skills for anyone planning to build a career. But deep expertise in physics, chemistry, biology and other disciplines remains equally important,” Mussin told the Kazinform news agency on the sidelines of the Olympiad.

His comments reflect a growing recognition that AI education increasingly extends beyond computer science itself, becoming a tool across multiple industries.

That approach is already shaping government policy. Kazakhstan has introduced artificial intelligence into university curricula and launched a national goal of training one million people in AI skills over the next five years, targeting students, civil servants, businesses and the broader workforce.

Infrastructure to match ambition

Education is only one component of Kazakhstan’s AI strategy. In recent months, the government has accelerated investments in digital infrastructure, commissioning Central Asia’s first advanced AI supercomputers, expanding satellite internet coverage through OneWeb and Starlink, signing agreements with Amazon’s Project Kuiper, and opening the International Center for Artificial Intelligence.

The country has also positioned itself more actively within global AI governance, becoming a founding member of the World Artificial Intelligence Cooperation Organization (WAICO), while securing major partnerships with NVIDIA and U.S.-based AI infrastructure company Firebird to develop large-scale computing infrastructure.

Together, these initiatives suggest Kazakhstan is attempting to build the foundations of an AI ecosystem rather than focusing solely on individual projects.

From digitalization to innovation

The broader question, however, is whether these investments can generate sustained innovation. As Indian Ambassador to Kazakhstan Y. K. Sailas Thangal noted in an earlier opinion article, artificial intelligence should be viewed not as an end in itself but as a tool capable of transforming healthcare, education, governance, agriculture and urban development when implemented responsibly.

That perspective aligns with Kazakhstan’s own strategy, which increasingly frames AI as an economy-wide technology rather than a standalone sector. Yet international experience suggests that building AI leadership requires more than digital infrastructure or educational reforms. Successful ecosystems typically depend on strong research universities, private investment, startup financing, commercialization pathways and the ability to retain highly skilled graduates.

Hosting an international Olympiad can raise a country’s profile. Turning that visibility into innovation, however, requires institutions capable of supporting talent long after the competition ends.

For Kazakhstan, the olympiad offers an opportunity to demonstrate how the country’s expanding investments in education, computing infrastructure and international partnerships fit into a broader national strategy.

World.title: Can Central Asia Turn Political Trust Into Lasting Regional Cooperation?
World.content:
ALMATY – Central Asia is moving beyond symbolic diplomacy toward a more durable system of regional coordination, according to Filippo Costa Buranelli, an associate professor of international relations at the University of St. Andrews in the United Kingdom. Following last week’s informal summit of Central Asian leaders and Azerbaijan in Cholpon-Ata, Buranelli said in an interview to the Baq.kz agency that the region has already built a stable political framework that now requires practical implementation through concrete mechanisms rather than new institutions.

His assessment comes after the July 31 meeting, where regional leaders adopted the Cholpon-Ata Declaration and discussed transport connectivity, energy, trade and regional security. During the meeting, President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev described the current period as the most successful in Central Asia’s modern history and proposed developing an action plan to implement the Treaty of Friendship, Good Neighborliness and Cooperation for the Development of Central Asia in the 21st Century.

From confidence-building to coordination

According to Buranelli, the region has entered a new phase.

“The political, economic and broader development environment is becoming more regular, predictable and coordinated,” he said, noting that the significance of the Cholpon-Ata meeting lies not only in its outcomes but also in the frequency of high-level consultations.

Unlike previous years, when regional meetings primarily served to rebuild trust after a prolonged period of limited interaction, Central Asian leaders now meet twice a year under the consultative format – one formal summit and one informal gathering.

While Buranelli does not believe the format is necessarily evolving into a traditional international organization, he argues that institutionalization should not be measured solely by the creation of permanent bureaucracies.

“What matters more is that a stable political and coordination framework has already emerged, allowing countries to promote mutual interests in a coordinated manner,” he said.

That evolution, he said, mirrors Kazakhstan’s own approach to regional diplomacy, which has consistently favored pragmatic cooperation over supranational integration.

Why Tokayev’s proposal matters

One of the summit’s most consequential initiatives may not have been the declaration itself, but Tokayev’s proposal to prepare an implementation plan for the regional friendship treaty. For Buranelli, this shifts the conversation from political commitments toward measurable action.

The treaty, signed by all five Central Asian states, establishes principles of good-neighborliness, peaceful dispute resolution and sustainable development. Unlike many regional agreements, it has no expiration date and does not require countries to transfer sovereignty or harmonize foreign policy.

Instead, it creates what Buranelli describes as a “legally grounded but flexible framework” capable of accommodating different political systems and national priorities.

“President Tokayev’s proposal to develop a concrete implementation plan for the treaty gives this architecture a practical dimension. Kazakhstan consistently promotes the approach that political agreements should be transformed into clear mechanisms, guidelines, and joint projects,” he said.

That approach, he argued, allows Central Asia to deepen cooperation without sacrificing the flexibility that has become one of the consultative format’s greatest strengths.

Azerbaijan expands the region’s strategic horizon

The summit also reflected a broader geographical shift.

Following Azerbaijan’s accession as a full participant, cooperation increasingly extends beyond the five Central Asian states toward the Caspian region. Rather than fundamentally changing the nature of the consultative format, Buranelli believes Azerbaijan broadens its practical scope. Thus, transport corridors, energy exports, digital connectivity and investment now link Central Asia more directly with the South Caucasus and European markets.

The development complements Kazakhstan’s long-standing efforts to strengthen the Trans-Caspian International Transport Route, or Middle Corridor, reducing dependence on traditional transit routes while diversifying access to global markets.

The expanding agenda also includes tourism, innovation, digitalization, artificial intelligence and space technologies, illustrating how regional cooperation is gradually moving beyond traditional security and trade issues.

From declarations to delivery

For Buranelli, the Cholpon-Ata summit suggests that Central Asia has largely solved the political problem that dominated the region only a decade ago: rebuilding trust among its neighbors. The more difficult phase is only beginning as the challenge is no longer whether the countries can meet or agree on common principles. The challenge is whether those principles become part of everyday governance and cooperation between the countries.

That means making coordination routine rather than summit-driven, strengthening cooperation among ministries, expert communities and regional authorities, and increasingly evaluating national projects through a regional perspective.

In that sense, Tokayev’s proposal to develop an implementation plan for the regional friendship treaty may prove more consequential than the declaration itself. Rather than creating new institutions, it seeks to make existing commitments operational.

The next opportunity to measure that progress will come on Oct. 8, when Central Asian leaders and Azerbaijan are scheduled to reconvene in Avaza, Turkmenistan. By then, attention is likely to shift from broad political statements toward whether governments have begun translating the treaty into concrete initiatives, timelines and joint projects.

World.title: Campaign Week in Review: Kazakhstan’s Kurultai Race from July 27 to Aug. 2
World.content:
ASTANA – This week’s election campaign roundup covers developments from July 27 to Aug. 2, when Kazakhstan’s political parties intensified voter outreach following the first nationally televised debate and held dozens of campaign events nationwide.

National televised debate draws public attention

One of the week’s key campaign events took place on July 29, when Qazaqstan TV hosted the first round of the national televised debates featuring representatives of the seven parties contesting the Kurultai elections.

The debate opened with two-minute statements from each party outlining why they are seeking seats in the Kurultai and presenting the main priorities of their election platforms. The second segment featured two common policy questions posed to all participants, while the final round adopted a face-to-face format, allowing party representatives to question one another.

According to preliminary results based on 15,876 online votes, Adilet received 66.1% support, followed by the Aq Jol Democratic Party with 13.1%, the People’s Party of Kazakhstan with 8.2%, and Respublica with 7.1%. The Nationwide Social Democratic Party (NSDP) garnered 2.8%, while Auyl received 2% and the Baytaq Green Party 0.3%. An additional 0.4% of respondents selected the None of the above option.

Adilet focuses on rural development

The Adilet party continued its nationwide campaign through its mobile caravan visiting the Atyrau, Karagandy, Akmola and North Kazakhstan regions.

Campaign events centered on infrastructure, public utilities, household incomes and rural development. Residents raised concerns over healthcare accessibility, road conditions, engineering infrastructure, agricultural support and opportunities for young people.

In the North Kazakhstan Region alone, residents submitted nearly 100 proposals for rural development, all of which the party said would be recorded for further consideration. The party also promoted initiatives aimed at expanding opportunities in sports, tourism and regional business while discussing industrial safety, enterprise modernization, workforce training, wage growth and the development of industrial towns.

Aq Jol highlights entrepreneurship

The Aq Jol Democratic Party launched campaign meetings in the Aktobe and Karagandy regions, presenting proposals to strengthen domestic manufacturing, support entrepreneurs, create jobs, improve tax policy and encourage industrial development.

In Aktobe, the party organized a Business Startup Forum, bringing together young entrepreneurs, banking representatives, IT specialists, development institutions, students and members of the business community.

Participants showcased startup projects and discussed financing mechanisms, innovation, cooperation with development institutions and ways to improve conditions for launching new businesses. Young entrepreneurs also shared proposals for expanding youth entrepreneurship.

Auyl promotes rural policy and women’s participation

The Auyl party met with labor collectives in the Kostanai Region, where representatives outlined proposals for rural development and discussed infrastructure, labor shortages and other social issues.

In Astana, the party also hosted a roundtable on the role of women in politics. Participants emphasized that meaningful influence on policymaking and budgeting is more important than the number of women holding office. Discussions also covered family support policies and expanding women’s participation in public life.

Baytaq centers campaign on environmental issues

The party continued to meet with workers across Kazakhstan while promoting environmental protection, public health, sustainable economic development, and stronger social support.

The Baytaq organized a cleanup campaign along the Shamalgan River in the Almaty Region and launched the Green LRT Branch campaign in Astana to promote environmentally friendly public transportation.

On July 28, World Nature Conservation Day, the party held a Car-Free Day, encouraging members to avoid private vehicles in favor of public transportation, the LRT, bicycles or walking.

On Aug. 2, the party officially launched its Baytaq environmental campaign caravan, beginning its route in the Aral Region.

People’s Party emphasizes historical memory

The People’s Party of Kazakhstan held a public music event in Almaty titled Eternal Classics, where classical music performances accompanied discussions with residents on current issues.

The party also focused on preserving historical memory, signing a cooperation memorandum with the Memorial Zone association to support search expeditions, archival research and patriotic education projects. Party representatives said preserving the memory of previous generations remains an important element of civic and patriotic education.

NSDP campaigns on social policy

The party continued focusing its campaign on vulnerable groups. Its representatives met with mothers raising children with chronic illnesses, including diabetes and celiac disease, in Uralsk; visited the Ulytau Meirimi support center for people with disabilities and a nursing home in Zhezkazgan; and met parents of children with disabilities in Pavlodar to present proposals supporting inclusive families.

The party’s campaign emphasized social welfare, including support for the inclusive community, the abolition of the compulsory social health insurance system, housing programs and pension reform.

NSDP also held a conference in Astana titled Problems of Modern Education, where participants discussed teacher shortages in special education, the disconnect between education and labor market needs, and transparency in science funding.

Respublica stresses regional development

The Respublica party held a supporters’ forum in Zhezkazgan, where participants discussed industrial development, road infrastructure, healthcare and education.

Party representatives visited enterprises in Zhezkazgan, Satpayev and the village of Kengir, meeting with workers to discuss increasing the share of small businesses in the regional economy and improving interregional freight transportation.

During campaign meetings, candidates also addressed regional challenges involving roads, healthcare, industry and education.

The discussion also featured criticism of the People’s Party of Kazakhstan for its proposal to impose penalties on schools with low PISA scores.

Respublica candidate Nurgul Tau argued that penalizing teachers would fail to address structural inequalities between rural and urban schools. Instead, she called for creating equal educational opportunities.

World.title: Georgian scam call centres: old fraudsters, new address? An investigation
World.content:
Georgian scam call centres that came under the spotlight during an international investigative project in 2025 have reportedly resumed operations from a new location. According to the investigative outlet Monitor, people linked to AK Group have relocated to an office at 68 Mirian Mepe Street in Tbilisi.

The outlet says its journalists conducted covert surveillance at the address for six months. They say they identified several of the same individuals who had been seen near AK Group’s previous office last year. According to Monitor, the footage also shows some of the same vehicles that regularly appeared at the company’s former location.

Journalists say they repeatedly spotted vehicles used by Akaki Kevkhishvili, who is widely believed to be the real operator of AK Group. The cars carried the registration numbers AK100KK and AK200KK. Investigators seized one of them in 2025 as part of the ongoing criminal investigation.

According to Monitor, AK Group’s registered owner and director, Meri Shotadze, also regularly visited the same address. She used two different vehicles, one of which investigators have also seized, while the other is registered to another person.

The investigation also claims that several agents who previously worked at AK Group’s former office have reappeared at the new location. They include Anzhelika Chkhapelia, who allegedly used the alias Marina Novikova; Misha Bayramov; Valerian Gigauri; Giorgi Gotman; and Ketevan Malashkhia, who allegedly used the alias Ashley Moriarty. According to Monitor, Malashkhia is a cousin of Akaki Kevkhishvili’s wife. The outlet also identified a Belarusian citizen, Lita, who had previously denied working at the call centre.

The journalists also say they identified security staff at the new office who had previously been seen outside AK Group’s former premises. They named former law enforcement officer Manuchar Gegia and former Zugdidi traffic police chief Levan Gogia.

According to the outlet, the office on Mirian Mepe Street closed after it announced the publication of its latest investigation. Both floors of the building are now being offered for rent.

Monitor says the premises had been leased since 2022 by RTM Imports, a company owned by Irakli Kvlividze, the brother of Akaki Kevkhishvili’s wife.

The journalists say they informed the Prosecutor’s Office on 1 July 2026 that AK Group’s managers and employees had been regularly operating from the office at 68 Mirian Mepe Street. According to Monitor, prosecutors have not clarified whether they investigated the information or whether the inquiry into the alleged fraud is still ongoing.

Background

In 2025, Monitor and more than 32 international media organisations published an investigation into AK Group’s activities. According to the report, the group employed 85 people and defrauded more than 6,100 people across Europe and Canada between 2022 and 2025. The journalists estimated that the operation generated more than $35 million in revenue over that period.

After the investigation was published, law enforcement authorities opened a criminal inquiry into organised fraud and the laundering of proceeds from crime on an especially large scale. Prosecutors have charged 11 people in the case.

In a separate bribery case, authorities also arrested former Georgian State Security Service chief Grigol Liluashvili. Prosecutors accuse him, in one of the counts, of providing protection to the call centres. A court has also frozen the assets and company shares of the alleged organisers and employees of the call centre network.

Investigation continues

According to Monitor, the Prosecutor’s Office told the outlet that it had requested legal assistance from Germany to help identify potential victims. Prosecutors also said they had sought additional information from journalists involved in the investigation, but claimed they had declined to cooperate.

In a written response, the Prosecutor’s Office said that “the final decision in the case largely depends on information and materials to be obtained from abroad through legal assistance.”

A separate Monitor investigation found that Akaki Kevkhishvili and Meri Shotadze had previously worked at another call centre, 100 Marketing Solutions. Authorities began investigating the company in 2023 and froze its shares as part of the inquiry. However, a court lifted the freeze in 2026.

Are Georgian scam call centres still operating?

World.title: Armenia approves new government as Pashinyan promises appointments based on merit
World.content:
Armenia approves new government

Alongside the opening of Armenia‘s 9th parliamentary term, the country formed a new government. In line with the constitution, Nikol Pashinyan took office as prime minister. He headed the electoral list of the Civil Contract party, which won a parliamentary majority.

The party submitted the required nomination documents for its leader to President Vahagn Khachaturyan, who then signed a decree appointing Pashinyan as prime minister.

On the previous day, at the proposal of Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan and by decree of President Vahagn Khachaturyan, Deputy Prime Ministers Mher Grigoryan and Tigran Khachatryan were reappointed to their posts.

Most cabinet ministers were also reappointed.

Changes were made in the prime minister’s office. Former chief adviser to the prime minister and former Armenian ambassador to the United States, Lilit Makunts, has been appointed chief of staff. Her predecessor, Araik Harutyunyan, became an MP with the ruling Civil Contract faction on August 2.

At the same time, Pashinyan announced that he plans to appoint graduates of leading universities from around the world, selected through the government’s talent pool, to senior positions in the government.

“You will soon see these decisions implemented in practice,” the prime minister said.

Almost all ministers kept their portfolios

At Prime Minister Pashinyan’s recommendation, the following ministers retained their posts:

Defence – Suren Papikyan,

Internal Affairs – Arpine Sargsyan,

Foreign Affairs – Ararat Mirzoyan,

Territorial Administration and Infrastructure – David Khudatyan,

Environment – Hambardzum Matevosyan,

Health – Anahit Avanesyan,

Education, Science, Culture and Sport – Zhanna Andreasyan,

Justice – Srbuhi Galyan,

Labour and Social Affairs – Arsen Torosyan,

Economy – Gevorg Papoyan,

Finance – Vahe Hovhannisyan.

Only High-Tech Industry Minister Mkhitar Hayrapetyan did not keep his post. Pashinyan had previously said that Hayrapetyan himself had decided to step down.

David Tadevosyan replaced him. The prime minister introduced the new minister to ministry staff today. Mkhitar Hayrapetyan also attended the meeting. He said he would remain available around the clock if the new minister or his team needed advice.

“I am ready to contribute my modest knowledge and experience whenever you feel the need,” the former minister said.

David Tadevosyan graduated from the National Polytechnic University of Armenia. Between 2012 and 2014, he studied at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT), where he earned a Master of Science in Engineering and Management.

Before taking up the ministerial post, Tadevosyan served as acting director of International Radio Network CJSC. Between 2024 and 2025, he headed Afeyan Initiatives for Armenia, an organisation founded by Armenian-American businessman, scientist and philanthropist Noubar Afeyan. Earlier in his career, Tadevosyan worked for the mining company Vallex Group, the Institute of Mining, Metallurgy and Chemical Technologies, and SberSpinoff.

More than 1,000 applications for the government’s talent pool

On 15 June, shortly after his Civil Contract party won the 2026 parliamentary elections, Armenian Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan invited graduates of the world’s leading universities to join the government. He encouraged them to put their knowledge and professional experience to work in public administration.

Today, the prime minister said the initiative had attracted strong interest, with the government receiving 1,141 applications.

“Following the initial screening, 459 candidates – around 40% of all applicants – advanced to the second stage. The average age of the candidates is 34,” Pashinyan said.

The prime minister announced that the government would create a talent pool based on interview results and professional assessments. Officials will match the selected candidates’ education, work experience and professional skills with the specific needs of the public administration system.

He added that candidates included in the talent pool could receive offers for positions in the public sector or other forms of cooperation during the course of this year.

Armenia approves new government

World.title: Opinion from Tbilisi: ‘It’s important to understand what kind of hell government is leading us into’
World.content:
Lasha Tugushi, head of the Liberal Academy, has commented on Georgian Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze’s claim that Georgian politicians have never used harsher rhetoric towards Russia than they do today, either before or after the 2008 war. Tugushi argues that the prime minister is repeating a familiar narrative promoted by the ruling Georgian Dream party.

According to Tugushi, the government is trying to present itself as the only force capable of “saving” the country, while linking the events of 2008 and 2022 forms part of that political strategy.

According to Tugushi, the suggestion that Georgia was ever pro-Russian is “nonsense”, as portraying Russia in a positive light has always been regarded as shameful in Georgian society.

Earlier, Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze published a lengthy social media statement linking the war in Ukraine to Georgia’s domestic politics and the country’s opposition. According to Kobakhidze, the “Global War Party” needed the war in Ukraine in order to “fuel Russophobia among its agents around the world, including in Georgia, at the highest level.”

Lasha Tugushi said: “Anti-Russian sentiment existed in Georgia long before this. I remember the 1990s, when hostility towards Russia was very strong. The same was true after the war in Abkhazia. I cannot agree with the prime minister’s view that the key turning points were 2008 and 2022.

“I do not remember Georgia ever being pro-Russian. That is nonsense. What’s more, in respectable society it has always been considered shameful to say that Russia is a good country or to speak positively about Russian symbols.

“As for the focus on 2008 and 2022, that is part of a political game in which the leaders of Georgian Dream repeat a familiar narrative: that there is only one benevolent political force capable of saving Georgia – Georgian Dream. Everyone else, they claim, is either an enemy or a traitor seeking to drag the country into a devastating war.”

“But let’s remember who suspended Georgia’s EU integration, who is pursuing an anti-European policy today, who is confronting the ambassadors of Western countries, the European Parliament and the OSCE, who is picking fights with Sweden and France. Who came up with the scare story about the ‘deep state’? Georgian Dream did all of that.

“That does not mean the previous government made no mistakes or that everything was perfect. We need to understand that politics cannot be viewed in black-and-white terms. Things should be called by their proper names. The previous government has plenty of its own sins, and it paid the price for them. But today we see countries that were once on a par with Georgia moving closer to EU membership, while we, instead of advancing towards integration, are drifting further away from the West.”

“There are two main pillars on which the current government relies.

The first is fear – the claim that enemies want to open a second front in Georgia.

The second is the argument that our Georgian identity is under threat.

These are the two narratives they use to frighten people and rely on a fearful public in order to remain in power indefinitely.

But the fact is that they are not succeeding in their campaign against democracy to the extent they would like. It is crucial to see clearly what kind of hell this government is leading us into and what it actually looks like.

Over the past few years, Georgian Dream has taken many steps backwards and not a single step forward. This is an anti-national path. It is building authoritarianism and working against the Georgian people. I have many questions. For example, can Georgian Dream correct the grave mistakes it has made? I would like to believe it can find that path and that at least something will change.”

On Georgian Dream’s policies

World.title: Georgian PM: ‘Opposition’s current Russophobia is dictated by Global War Party’
World.content:
Georgian Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze has published a lengthy social media statement linking Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine to Georgia‘s domestic politics and the country’s opposition.

According to Kobakhidze, the “Global War Party” needed the war in Ukraine in order to “fuel Russophobia among its agents around the world, including in Georgia, at the highest level.”

Kobakhidze writes that after the war in Ukraine began in 2022, the “opposition’s pseudo-liberal minority” in Georgia adopted a radical stance towards Russia. He argues that such attitudes had not existed even after the August 2008 war, despite the fact that Russia continued to occupy 20% of Georgia’s territory.

In his statement, the prime minister recalls the consequences of the 2008 war. He says Russia’s military aggression killed 412 people, injured 2,232 others and displaced about 30,000 people. More than 120 Georgian settlements also remained beyond the occupation line.

Kobakhidze argues that the United National Movement, which was in power at the time, did not pursue a hard-line policy towards Russia. Instead, he says, it encouraged Russian tourists and investors to come to Georgia, promoted cultural and economic ties, facilitated Russian investment in various sectors and later unilaterally abolished visa requirements for Russian citizens.

According to the prime minister, neither government officials nor their supporters protested against that policy at the time. In this context, Kobakhidze names several current opposition politicians and public figures, including Elene Khoshtaria and Zurab Japaridze, and claims they supported closer relations with Russia during that period.

According to the prime minister, the opposition, along with affiliated NGOs and activists, turned into an “externally controlled network of agents” and adopted a sharply anti-Russian stance only after Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.

Kobakhidze argues that the Georgian opposition’s current “Russophobia” is not genuine but stems from “directives issued by external forces”. He says that if anyone were to develop a truly radical attitude towards Russia, it should have happened after the August 2008 war, not after Russia’s second invasion of Ukraine.

The prime minister concludes his statement by asking why this “network of agents” did not display the same attitude towards Russia after the 2008 war, but only after the war in Ukraine began. Kobakhidze says society “will easily find a logical explanation” for that question.

“I believe there is a question that must be asked and carefully considered by society. We all know that, both in the past and today, this network of agents in Georgia has acted on instructions from external forces, and that its homeland is not Georgia but the ‘deep state’.

Against that backdrop, it is worth asking why they were not instructed to promote Russophobia when there was the strongest possible reason to do so – after the August 2008 war – and why they have been instructed to do so now, when the victim of Russian aggression is not their formal homeland but another country, albeit a friendly one. I believe society will easily find a logical explanation for this contradiction,” Kobakhidze wrote.

Kobakhidze on Russophobia in Georgia

World.title: Diaspora youth: Patriots or ‘information soldiers’? The hidden mission of camp in Azerbaijan
World.content:
Zangilan diaspora youth camp in Azerbaijan

Zangilan diaspora youth camp in Azerbaijan. More than 120 young people from 64 countries gathered in Zangilan under the slogan “Reviving Cities”. Officials told participants they should defend Azerbaijan’s achievements and push back against what they described as “biased campaigns”.

Against the backdrop of protesters calling Ilham Aliyev a “dictator” in Berlin, that message raises another question: is the state seeking to foster independent thinkers or “information soldiers” who will promote its official narrative abroad?

What was discussed at the 7th Diaspora Youth Summer Camp?

The 7th Diaspora Youth Summer Camp, which opened in Zangilan on 2 August, is officially presented as a platform for “patriotic education”, learning about “the realities on the ground” and rejuvenating the Azerbaijani diaspora. More than 120 young people from 64 countries are spending a week visiting reconstruction projects in the territories retaken by Azerbaijan, meeting government officials and learning what organisers describe as “Azerbaijani realities”.

A closer look at the speeches by Fuad Muradov, chairman of the State Committee for Work with the Diaspora, and other officials, however, reveals a more pragmatic objective. The government appears to see young people living abroad not simply as members of the diaspora with ties to their homeland, but as active participants in the information battle.

Muradov said the participants should be able to “respond with well-founded arguments to biased campaigns”. He said they should “represent” Azerbaijan’s interests with dignity in their countries of residence, on international platforms and within their own communities.

Another message struck an even tougher tone. Officials said that although their number was small, some people living abroad who called themselves Azerbaijanis did not welcome Azerbaijan’s successes. They urged participants to know who these people were, be familiar with their statements and respond to them with well-reasoned arguments. Officials also said “black PR”, “distortion of facts” and “organised campaigns” were unacceptable. At the same time, they said they remained open to “well-founded criticism”.

Elvin Aslanov, a representative of the Heydar Aliyev Foundation, acknowledged that defending Azerbaijan abroad was “far from easy”, saying it required confronting double standards and disinformation. According to him, the young participants’ mission is to “convey the truth accurately and objectively”.

From the authorities’ perspective, such rhetoric may appear defensive and entirely legitimate. However, the broader context allows for another interpretation. Critics argue that the programme goes beyond patriotic education and instead systematically prepares “information soldiers” – young people expected to promote the official narrative on social media, in online discussions and in international debates. In other words, they see it as an attempt to build a state-directed “soft power” network.

What happened in Berlin, and why does it matter in this context?

The timing of these appeals is no coincidence. During Ilham Aliyev’s official visit to Germany on 21 July, Azerbaijani expatriates gathered on the streets of Berlin and chanted: “Dictator!”

Around the same time, Germany-based exiled blogger Alemdar Bunyatov approached Foreign Minister Jeyhun Bayramov and presidential aide Hikmet Hajiyev on a street in Berlin. He questioned them about political prisoners and allegations of torture.

Official media immediately described the incident as a “provocation” and portrayed Bunyatov as someone “known for his close ties to the Iranian intelligence services”. Responding to his questions, Bayramov dismissed the allegations of torture as “a personal opinion”.

Hajiyev, for his part, questioned Bunyatov about his sources of funding, his legal status in Germany and his reasons for leaving Azerbaijan. He stressed the importance of sovereignty and national security. The incident triggered a strong reaction in pro-government media, which portrayed the blogger’s questions as “provocative”.

The events in Berlin further illustrate the practical meaning of the messages delivered in Zangilan. In the official narrative, criticism is often framed as a “biased campaign”, “black PR” or the result of “external influence”.

As a result, the authorities themselves largely determine the line between “well-founded criticism” and a “biased campaign”. Young people, in turn, are expected to accept that distinction and challenge those whom the state places on the other side of it.

A method of training trolls?

Opposition figures and independent observers have long described such camps as a form of “troll factory”. Critics argue that their purpose is not to encourage independent thinking but to prepare young people to defend the official position on social media, in online discussions and before international audiences. They say that, under the banner of patriotism, organisers cultivate emotional attachment and ideological loyalty while encouraging participants to view critical voices as “hostile”.

Every country seeks to use its diaspora as a tool of soft power, and Azerbaijan is no exception. The problem, critics argue, is that the shrinking space for domestic criticism places a disproportionately heavy burden on young Azerbaijanis abroad to “defend” the official line. They must adapt to societies where freedom of expression is a fundamental principle while remaining loyal to Baku’s official narrative. For many young people, that contradiction can create genuine tension.

Muradov says, “We are open to dialogue”, while also insisting, “We will not tolerate black PR.” This raises an obvious question: what qualifies as “well-founded criticism”, and what counts as a “biased campaign”? If official media portray the questions and slogans heard on the streets of Berlin as a provocation, where is the line for young people who raise the same issues in international media or at academic forums?

Zangilan diaspora youth camp in Azerbaijan

World.title: Armenia’s new parliament holds first session as opposition, as expected, makes its presence felt
World.content:
First session of Armenia’s ninth parliament

Armenia‘s newly elected parliament convened for the first time on 2 August. Three political forces won seats in the ninth National Assembly: the Civil Contract, Strong Armenia and Armenia factions. During the opening session, lawmakers managed only to appoint members of the Counting Commission. Heated exchanges between the ruling party and the opposition prevented them from addressing the rest of the agenda.

The opposition’s main grievance was the absence of the Catholicos from the opening session. The authorities did not invite him, and he did not bless the work of parliament. Opposition lawmakers described this as an unprecedented event in the history of independent Armenia.

Under the constitutional law governing the National Assembly’s rules of procedure, both the president and the Catholicos of All Armenians have the right to deliver opening remarks at parliament’s first session. This time, however, only President Vahagn Khachaturyan addressed lawmakers. Earlier, the Mother See of Holy Etchmiadzin said it had received no invitation for the Catholicos. When journalists asked Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan about Garegin II’s participation, he replied: “I do not know such a Catholicos.” The incident reflects the long-running dispute between the Armenian authorities and Catholicos of All Armenians Garegin II. More than two years ago, Prime Minister Pashinyan called for the Catholicos to step down. He initially argued that Garegin II could not lead the Armenian Apostolic Church because he had broken his vow of celibacy and fathered a daughter. Pashinyan later accused him of links with foreign intelligence services. The ruling Civil Contract party also included the removal of “the de facto head of the Church” in its election manifesto.

Lawmakers also fiercely debated the nomination of Ruben Rubinyan, the ruling party’s sole candidate for speaker of parliament.

Opposition MPs repeatedly referred to his research work at Istanbul Policy Center in Turkey in 2017–18. They asked whether he had interacted with local residents and even questioned what they looked like.

“Ask me directly whether I met representatives of the Turkish intelligence services in Turkey and whether they recruited me. Ask me: ‘Is that true?’ And I will answer: ‘No,'” Rubinyan said.

Parliament resumed its first session today. Lawmakers have already settled one of the main items on the agenda. In a secret ballot, they elected Ruben Rubinyan as speaker with 63 votes in favour and 28 against.

The opposition Armenia bloc boycotted the secret ballot. MPs from the second opposition force, the Strong Armenia faction, voted against Rubinyan’s nomination.

In the previous parliament, Rubinyan served as deputy speaker. Between 2022 and 2026, he also acted as Armenia’s special envoy for the normalisation of relations with Turkey. A few days ago, Rubinyan said he would be unable to continue in that role if parliament elected him speaker. The ruling party has not yet announced who will succeed him.

“Where is the Patriarch?” Opposition MPs visit him to receive his blessing

On the opening day of the session, opposition MPs began chanting, “Where is the Patriarch?” after the president’s address. During the oath-taking ceremony, they pointedly refused to stand or recite the oath. They said they were protesting the Catholicos’s absence. However, they signed the written text of the oath, allowing them to take office formally.

At the end of the first working day, MPs from both opposition factions visited the Catholicos’s residence.

The Mother See’s information service said Garegin II blessed the opposition lawmakers. He spoke of an “alarming situation and serious problems” facing the country. He also criticised what he described as the authorities’ “illegal and unconstitutional actions” against the Church.

Catholicos receives opposition MPs at the Mother See

The Catholicos praised what he described as the opposition MPs’ “devotion and filial love for the Church”. He said their stance was especially important at a time when “the authorities continue their campaign of repression, while national benefactor Samvel Karapetyan remains under arrest for speaking out in defence of Holy Etchmiadzin”.

In June last year, Armenian authorities opened a criminal case against Russian businessman and billionaire Samvel Karapetyan. Prosecutors accused him of publicly calling for the seizure and usurpation of power. In an interview with local media, Karapetyan discussed the escalating conflict between the government and the Church. He said he supported the Church and added: “If Armenia’s political forces fail to resolve this situation, we will have to intervene in the campaign against the Church in our own way.” His supporters founded the Strong Armenia party after his arrest, and he has remained under house arrest since December last year.

105 MPs in the new parliament

The three political forces that entered the National Assembly secured the following number of seats:

The ruling Civil Contract party – 64 seats

The Strong Armenia faction – 29 seats

The Armenia bloc – 12 seats

Strong Armenia leader and businessman Samvel Karapetyan did not enter parliament. During the election campaign, his allies confidently predicted victory and even said Karapetyan would become prime minister. However, he is ineligible to serve either as an MP or as prime minister. Under Armenia’s constitution, anyone holding citizenship of another country cannot hold either office. Karapetyan holds Armenian, Russian and Cypriot citizenship.

Former President Robert Kocharyan headed the electoral list of the Armenia bloc, making him its candidate for prime minister. However, Kocharyan declined to take up his parliamentary seat. His son, Levon Kocharyan, who also ran on the bloc’s list, accepted a mandate and has already joined parliament. He also served as an MP for the Armenia bloc in the previous legislature.

“I will do everything to ensure our children never experience war”

Rubinyan thanked the more than 700,000 voters who backed Civil Contract. He said they had given the ruling party “a mandate to continue Armenia’s democratic reforms and peace agenda”. According to Rubinyan, those voters had defended the country’s sovereignty and independence.

He said the time had come for Armenians to enjoy peaceful lives, have children and raise them without fear.

“My son, who is almost two years old, and children of his age have never experienced war. I will do everything to ensure that my children, your children and all our children never have to learn what war is,” he said.

Rubinyan also thanked those who voted for opposition parties out of conviction rather than in exchange for election bribes.

“It is time to change the political discourse,” Rubinyan says

Addressing opposition MPs, Rubinyan raised the issue of the tone of parliamentary debate. He said society, political circles and journalists had formed a common view of parliament in recent months. According to him, many now see the National Assembly as a place for pointless arguments, slander and insults.

“They say this parliament will be even worse than the previous one in that respect. It seems everyone expects exactly that from us. I want to propose that we break this curse together,” the speaker said.

He argued that the opposition factions had largely stayed away from the work of the previous, eighth convocation of parliament.

“All we saw here was political confrontation, shouting and radical speeches. It is time to change the narratives that have dominated Armenian politics over the past six years. I propose that we make this parliament a place for vigorous but respectful debate that never crosses the boundaries of decency.”

At the same time, he warned that if the opposition rejected his proposal and continued “down the well-trodden path”, the ruling party was ready to respond “in the toughest possible way”.

“Why did we take our seats?” Opposition MPs explain

Ishkhan Saghatelyan, an MP from the Armenia faction, argued that neither the opposition nor the ruling party had truly won the election.

He again claimed that the authorities had used administrative resources during the campaign and imprisoned opposition figures.

“This parliament has a serious legitimacy problem. We are here to organise political struggle and advance national goals. We are here to raise the concerns of Armenia’s citizens, speak about the prisoners held in Baku and Armenia’s occupied territories, and, yes, defend the people of Artsakh’s right to a collective return.”

Hayk Farmanyan, an MP from the Strong Armenia faction, echoed that message.

“We accepted our mandates to remain true to our Armenian identity, to fight for our national values, and to defend our dignity, our identity and our Church.”

Comment

Political analyst Lilit Dallakyan shared her impressions of the new parliament’s opening session on social media:

“Well, I ‘congratulate’ the Armenian people on the start of work by a new, high-quality, substantive parliament that is supposedly ready to tackle Armenia’s complex challenges.

The daily exchange of ‘Your father is a murderer’ [directed at MP Levon Kocharyan, son of former President Robert Kocharyan] will now gain a new, equally substantive argument: ‘Your uncle is a Russian oligarch’ [directed at MP Narek Karapetyan, nephew of Strong Armenia leader Samvel Karapetyan]. That will, in turn, prompt the reply: ‘You are Turkish dictators’ [directed at the authorities].

The only positive aspect is that this season of the series is unlikely to interest anyone or distract people from the real problems that are rapidly emerging.

At a time of profound change across the world, Armenian society and every individual will have to look for solutions to their own problems. Ultimately, that will bring about the changes the country needs.”

First session of Armenia’s ninth parliament

World.title: Opinion: ‘Abkhaz diplomacy must become more flexible – and more assertive’
World.content:
Against the backdrop of the Pacific island nation of Nauru withdrawing its recognition of Abkhazia’s independence, prominent Abkhaz public figure Akhra Bzhania reflects on what Abkhazia’s foreign policy doctrine should look like.

Nauru, a small island nation in the Pacific region of Micronesia, recognised Abkhazia’s independence in 2009 but withdrew that recognition in late July 2026. The move reduced the number of countries recognising Abkhazia’s independence to four. Abkhazia’s foreign ministry said Nauru had come under “unprecedented pressure”.

Akhra Bzhania said: “Around 230,000 irregular migrants crossed the EU’s borders in 2025–26 alone. All of them fled countries that enjoy broad international recognition.

Why didn’t they stay in Morocco, Mali or Afghanistan? Presumably because having a flag outside the UN headquarters does not automatically mean you live in a genuine state – one where you can influence public life, where your voice matters and where your dignity will never be trampled.

Being a recognised country and being a country where people want to live and are willing to die for it are two different things.

You may achieve the first and never attain the second. But if you have the second, then you have accomplished the most important task: building a country that belongs to its citizens. That is what defines a modern state. And that is precisely what should become the main instrument for Abkhazia’s integration into the international community.

Bzhania continued: “We must send a clear message to the international community that, despite sanctions, isolation and the threat of war, the people of Abkhazia have built a society based on the rule of law and freedom. Without being members of international institutions, we have incorporated the core principles of international conventions on civil and political rights into our system of governance.

We see ourselves as part of the international community and believe we deserve our rightful place within it. To achieve that, our diplomacy must become more flexible – and more assertive. It should focus not on waiting for or preserving acts of recognition, but on consistently demonstrating our statehood and expanding our international contacts.

No one else is obliged to do this for us. By recognising our sovereignty, Russia effectively made Abkhazia a subject of international law. But it cannot solve our problems on our behalf.”

Bzhania continued: “We must use every tool at our disposal to achieve our goals: the resources of the diaspora, cultural, trade and sporting ties, personal connections, migration policy and regional logistics. In this game, we need to keep raising the stakes.

Today, there is a window of opportunity for such an active policy. It is no secret that relations between Georgia and the West are at their lowest point since the 1990s. Those on whom Tbilisi relied to promote its anti-Abkhaz agenda have become disillusioned with Georgia, and we should take advantage of that. That includes reviving the active dialogue with European countries that existed in the late 1990s. After all, the hopes the West once placed in Georgia as a bastion of the free world in the Caucasus have, to a greater extent, been realised in Abkhazia.

Another key asset, which has remained almost entirely outside our foreign policy efforts, is the Circassian diaspora. Four million people spread across 50 countries represent a powerful resource we can genuinely rely on. More importantly, we should offer them the prospect of political cooperation.

Abkhazia can and should become the centre of the Circassian world as the only independent state of this sub-ethnic group. Our country can become the same kind of homeland for Circassians worldwide that Israel has become for Jews. If every Circassian, wherever they live, knows they will find protection and support for their interests in Abkhazia, it will create a strong foundation for advancing our shared interests.”

Bzhania concluded: “It will probably not happen tomorrow, no matter how much effort we put in. But it can happen within a foreseeable future if those efforts remain consistent and systematic.

In 2017, I had the honour of welcoming a delegation from Nauru’s parliament to Abkhazia on behalf of the Abkhaz parliament. They were wonderful, warm people. Unfortunately, ships at sea do not only meet – they also part ways. Today, Nauru has set a course away from Abkhazia, apparently believing it to be the safer option. I wish them well. As for us, we will continue on our own course.”

The terminology, place names and views expressed in this article are those of the author and do not necessarily reflect the editorial position of this website.

Nauru’s withdrawal of recognition of Abkhazia

World.title: “For safe and strong Georgia”: Saturday march in Tbilisi. Georgia protests video blog
World.content:
612th day of protests in Tbilisi

“For a Safe and Strong Georgia” was the main slogan of the traditional pro-European Saturday march held in Tbilisi on 1 August 2026.

Before the march began, participants observed a minute’s silence in memory of a teenager who was recently killed in central Tbilisi and who would have turned 18 today.

Hundreds of people gathered once again in Avlabari Square for the 612th consecutive day of protests. With construction work continuing on Rustaveli Avenue, the march followed an alternative route for the second Saturday in a row, starting at Avlabari metro station and ending outside the parliament building.

For more than a year and half – since November 2024 – continuous protests have been taking place in Georgia, with demonstrators demanding that the country return to the path of European integration. Every evening thousands, and often tens of thousands, gather in Tbilisi and several other cities. Over this time dozens of participants have been detained, many have faced criminal charges, and some have been sentenced to prison terms. For the first time in the history of independent Georgia, the country has up to 150 prisoners of conscience, including women. Among them is Mzia Amaglobeli, founder of the popular outlets Batumelebi and Netgazeti. In 2025 she was sentenced to two years in prison for slapping a police officer. Protesters demand the release of all political prisoners, new parliamentary elections – as they do not recognize the results of the 2024 vote – and the repeal of all anti-democratic laws adopted over the past two years. To suppress the protests, the ruling Georgian Dream party has increasingly tightened repression against civil society and the media. However, protests in various forms continue.

612th day of protests in Tbilisi

World.title: Calls to permanently open historic tunnel in Sydney's Blue Mountains
World.content:
Blue Mountains City Council wants $15 million to permanently reopen a 134-year-old tunnel that drew sell-out crowds at the weekend.

Originally built for a railway to the mountains in 1892, the Lapstone Hill Tunnel once stored munitions and mustard gas during World War II and at one point served as a mushroom farm.

Mayor Mark Greenhill says council spent $4 million from a state government grant to clean out the tunnel and install lighting.

Council want to open the tunnel permanently as a tourist attrtaction and walking route. (Supplied: Blue Mountains City Council)

However, he says further funding is needed to build car parking and easy access and exit to the site.

"What we're seeking is partnership from the other levels of government so that this really amazing piece of Australia's history can be opened up permanently," Cr Greenhill said.

" It is like walking back in time to another era. "

Cr Greenhill says the council has a temporary lease on the state-owned site which is due to end by the end of the year.

The Lapstone Hill Tunnel was originally conceived as a railway tunnel through the Lapstone monocline. (Supplied: Blue Mountains City Council)

"My fear is this, if we don't get some funding by the end of the year, the license will finish. All the work we've done will be for naught," Cr Greenhill said.

"All the work we've done to clean it up, put lights in it, it'll have been for nothing and might be locked away for another couple of centuries."

The council argues opening the tunnel would provide a safer cycling route between Western Sydney and the Blue Mountains, potentially removing cyclists from the Great Western Highway between Glenbrook and Lapstone.

The state heritage-listed tunnel was opened in 1892 as a railway tunnel in the Blue Mountains, but was later closed in 1913 because it was too steep for trains.

Lapstone local David Watson says the tunnel represents a "missing link" for cyclists. (Supplied: Blue Mountains City Council)

Locals back permanent opening

Thousands of residents and visitors attended open days over the last two weekends, which allowed for walk-throughs of the historic tunnel.

David Watson grew up in Lapstone and remembers the tunnel portals being a scary place because they were locked up and inaccessible.

He started campaigning to open the tunnel in 2012 after seeing the portals surrounded by disused shipping containers and forklifts from its days as a mushroom farm.

""This would be a perfect thing for people to walk through with their dogs or their kids and for push bikes to ride through," Mr Watson said.

" This is like a missing link that would … get cyclists off the busy highway but also get walkers back into the lower mountains. "

Lapstone local Michele Corin said the tunnel was inspiring a sense of wonder in Blue Mountains residents who turned up in droves.

"It's a place that brings people together, strengthens local identity and showcases the heritage that shaped our region," Ms Corin said.

A spokesperson for the Department of Planning, Housing and Infrastructure said the state government would support the council's efforts to activate the site "while pursuing alternate funding sources".

"The NSW Government previously provided $4 million to Blue Mountains City Council for remediation of the Lapstone Tunnel," the spokesperson said.

World.title: Boy's sore throat leads to leukaemia diagnosis
World.content:
A Sunshine Coast mother says her 10-year-old son is devastated to be spending his next birthday in hospital after a persistent sore throat led to his leukaemia diagnosis.

Naomi Turner, a Bli Bli photographer and mother of four, said in hindsight her son Cooper's drop in energy levels was the first sign something was not right.

"He was so quiet," she said.

Naomi Turner is devastated by her son Cooper's cancer diagnosis. (Supplied: Turner family/ Hello Honey Photography)

"Normally he would run in, throw his bag in the door, grab a snack and run up to the neighbours and play footy with them all afternoon.

"Whereas we'd come home and he'd just sit at the table."

Sore throat worsens

It started about three weeks ago when Cooper woke up with an "extreme sore throat" and said he did not want to go to school.

"For any kid, [that's] quite normal, not out of the blue," Ms Turner said.

After a trip to the doctor, he was prescribed antibiotics for a suspected case of tonsillitis.

When those did not work, and the pain worsened, his mother took him to hospital and then back again to the doctor the following week.

"It was still severe. He wasn't eating … he wasn't even walking," Ms Turner said.

Cooper Turner loves playing sports with his friends. (Supplied: Turner family)

After more doctor appointments, Cooper was again seen at Sunshine Coast University Hospital's emergency department on the morning of July 27.

By 9am the next day, he was undergoing chemotherapy at the Brisbane Children's Hospital for acute myeloid leukaemia.

"He was quite critical," Ms Turner said.

She said it was a "complete shock" when doctors delivered the news.

"I went blank at first," Ms Turner said through tears.

"Then I just began shaking."

Head of Mater Research's blood cancer research group, Maher Gandhi, said infections were a common symptom of leukaemia.

"Infections can present in many ways, but a sore throat is one of the commonest ways," Professor Gandhi said.

Maher Gandhi says infections are common symptoms of cancer. (Supplied: Maher Gandhi)

"I wouldn't want to cause a lot of undue alarm because most common childhood illnesses, like sore throats, are nothing related to leukaemia at all."

Symptoms to watch out for

Professor Gandhi said to look out for recurrent sore throats, if the sore throats persisted for a long time, if they were very severe, and particularly if they were related to other symptoms such as low energy.

He said children were usually "quite active" and if a child lost interest in a sport or activity they usually enjoyed, or were out of breath easily, it could be an indicator.

Cooper Turner had a sore throat that turned out to be cancer. (Supplied: Turner family)

"Sometimes the child is less interested in things that would normally get them quite excited and that might be friendships, something happening at school, it might be a family activity, and it might be sport or some kind of entertainment that suggests they're just a bit tired and uninterested," Professor Gandhi said.

He also said headaches, bruising easily, bleeding gums, fevers, lumps, joint or bone pain, and nose bleeds could be an issue.

Six months in hospital

Now in hospital, Ms Turner said Cooper was low on energy and spent most of his time in bed or undergoing treatment.

His treatment plan is expected to take six months, depending on how his body reacts to it.

Naomi Turner says it is important to keep seeking medical advice for your children if something does not seem right. (Supplied: Turner family/ Hello Honey Photography)
