"It is so hard to watch," Ms Turner said.

"Just heartbreaking."

Seeking medical advice

Although acute myeloid leukaemia is known to occur in children, Professor Gandhi reiterated cancer in general was "uncommon in children".

"This kind of cancer occurs because the machinery of the bone marrow isn't working so well," he said.

"[It] is more likely to occur in older people.

Cooper Tuner will be in hospital undergoing treatment for the next six months. (Supplied: Turner family)

"Most of the symptoms that I've talked about are not due to leukaemia. It's really if the symptoms persist for a long time, then it is worth taking your child to the GP."

Ms Turner's advice for other parents was to proactively seek medical advice.

"If you feel like something is wrong … fight for it," she said.

World.title: Prisoners paid compensation for sleeping on floor amid overcrowding
World.content:
Prisoners are receiving financial compensation to sleep on the floor in overcrowded Western Australian jails, the ABC can reveal.

The overcrowding across the state's prison system, described by a Supreme Court Justice as "significant and inhumane", has also resulted in reduced sentences for criminals convicted of serious offences.

The Department of Justice has confirmed prisoners with "alternative sleeping arrangements", including sleeping on mattresses on the floor in cramped cells, are receiving a gratuity payment of up to $10.15 per week.

A gratuity payment is normally awarded to prisoners if they engage in meaningful activities such as work and education programs, and the amount they are paid depends on the level of skill or effort involved.

Overcrowding has led to mattresses being placed on the floor at prisions across the state, including in Broome. (Supplied: OICS)

In a statement, the department did not answer questions about when the payment was introduced for this purpose, or in which prisons it was occurring.

"The gratuity has been a long-standing administrative practice while managing prison population pressures," the statement said.

"The number of prisoners receiving the payment varies from day to day depending on the number of prisoners accommodated in alternative sleeping arrangements across the prison system."

Overcrowding in WA's prisons has become a growing issue in recent years. (ABC Midwest and Wheatbelt: Cecile O'Connor)

Up to 200 adult inmates had slept on mattresses on the floor across the state's prison system throughout 2026, as of June, despite 'triple-bunking' in over 250 cells.

What can the payments be used for? Purchasing items from the prison canteen

Buying special-order items authorised by the superintendent

Placed into the prisoner's savings account

Prisoners may also apply for the transfer of gratuities into the bank account of a registered visitor, such as a family member, if there is a legitimate reason, such as financial hardship.

Government has 'lost control' of prisons

Shadow Corrective Services Minister Adam Hort said gratuity payments for those sleeping on the floor did not occur under the last Liberal government, which was last in power in 2017.

Adam Hort says paying inmates a gratuity payment to be in prison "makes no sense to anyone". (ABC News: Samantha Goerling)

"These payments are absolutely an admission that Roger Cook has lost control of our prison system, that he would have to pay prisoners to stay in these overcrowded prison cells," he said.

" No taxpayer would ever expect a government to pay prisoners a gratuity payment to be in prison. That makes no sense to anyone. "

Overcrowding leading to reduced sentences

Supreme Court Justice Alain Musikanth last month ruled that the "significant and inhumane overcrowding" at Hakea Prison was a mitigating factor when sentencing Mihael Vrhovsek to 16 years' jail for attempted murder, meaning the harsh prison conditions reduced the severity of his punishment.

Man jailed for attempted murder A man who "doggedly" tried to kill a woman in a prolonged attack in suburban Perth caught on CCTV is jailed for 16 years.

Vrhovsek tried to kill a woman outside a Perth apartment complex in a horrific attack captured on CCTV.

It was revealed in court Vrhovsek was receiving "modest financial compensation" due to "unacceptable overcrowding" at Hakea Prison.

"Your counsel spoke this morning of the real hardship which you have suffered and are likely still to suffer while being incarcerated in prison, particularly in Hakea Prison, in circumstances where there is a chronic shortage of space, significant and inhumane overcrowding," Justice Musikanth said.

"It would seem to me that this is a form of hardship that regrettably operates largely across the board."

An image of a cell with three beds at Hakea Prison in Perth, from a scathing report from the Office of the Inspector of Custodial Services. (Supplied: Office of the Inspector of Custodial Services)

It was not the fist time overcrowding at Hakea was cited as a mitigating factor in sentencing.

In September 2025, District Court Judge Linda Black reduced the sentence of Laban Joshua Toga Saininaivalu, convicted of attempted possession of cocaine with intent to sell or supply, due to what she described as "horrendous" conditions, with "severe overcrowding".

Judge Black said the conditions at Hakea Prison were so far below the expected standard and so "intolerable" that time spent inside the prison should be "weighted more heavily".

Growing prison population

In June, the Inspector of Custodial Services Eamon Ryan issued a show cause notice — effectively a demand for the government to explain itself — over overcrowded conditions inside Hakea, Casuarina and Melaleuca prisons that he described as "cruel, inhumane and degrading".

Damning report on state of WA prisons WA prisoners are being subjected to "cruel, inhumane or degrading treatment" because the state government has allowed prisons to become "almost fundamentally broken", according to the Inspector of Custodial Services.

At the core of the problem, Mr Ryan said, was a 37 per cent increase in the prison population since early 2023, without a corresponding growth in the number of cells or prison staff.

He noted the biggest increase was in remand prisoners — people who were waiting for their cases to progress through the courts.

The average time in prison before being sentenced had grown from 188 days at the start of 2021 to 705 days at the start of this year.

As a result, on any given day most prisons were operating close to or above capacity.

Paul Papalia, who was the corrective services minister at the time, attributed the rising prison population to a growing general population, and a harder line being taken by WA Police and courts on family and domestic violence (FDV) offenders.

Payments do not fix overcrowding

The Acting Inspector of Custodial Services Jane Higgens said the real issue was not the gratuity payments, but rather the condition prisoners were kept in.

Report highlights Broome prison 'unfit for purpose' A damning report by Western Australia's prison watchdog dubs Broome Regional Prison "unfit for purpose".

"Compensation does not address overcrowding or its broader impacts," she said.

"A sustainable response requires reducing population pressures and ensuring prisons can provide safe, decent, and lawful conditions."

Monitoring of Hakea, Casuarina and Melaleuca prisons had shown some improvement, such as increased out-of-cell time, Ms Higgens said, but these improvements remained vulnerable to ongoing staff shortages, population growth and overcrowding.

Call for solutions

Law Society WA president Judy McClean said overcrowding could impact access to important services.

"If you can't get the offender the accurate or the appropriate services to rehabilitate while they are incarcerated, upon release you may find that they haven't addressed some of the issues or the concerns that underlie much of the offence," she said.

Social Reinvestment WA chief executive Sophie Stewart said there were practical solutions available to the government, and called for "an immediate injection of funds to create more staff, so that the prisons can safely and humanely function and people can get out of cells".

Sophie Stewart says the government has levers it can pull to alleviate the crisis. (ABC Kimberley: Giulia Bertoglio)

She also called on the state government to invest in more prison farms, bail and transition houses, residential alcohol and drug rehabilitation centres and more community mental health beds.

World.title: Live: Bridget McKenzie says 'widow tax' fix amounts to 'backflip'
World.content:
Environment and Water Minister Murray Watt has confirmed an independent review is underway into the Bureau of Meteorology.

The review, commissioned by the Bureau's CEO Stuart Minchin in consultation with Watt, will look at how the Bureau can best meet the needs of Australians.

Last year, it was inundated with feedback after rolling out a new $96 million website upgrade.

Watt says the review's findings will help guide future strategy.

World.title: Fears bird flu could have 'devastating' effect on Phillip Island penguins
World.content:
Environmentalists are concerned about "devastating effects" on Phillip Island's penguin colony and other wildlife as bird flu cases continue to spread throughout the state.

The major tourism hub, located around two hours south of Melbourne, is home to penguins, seals, and other animals susceptible to the bird flu strain taking hold across the country.

Victoria's first case of H5N1 was confirmed at Portland on the state's far south-west coast last week.

There are now seven confirmed cases in Victoria.

At least 78 cases of the virus have been confirmed across Australia, after the first case was detected in Western Australia in June.

Environment Victoria nature campaigns manager Chris Schuringa said if the H5 bird flu reached the island, it could cause "mass deaths" of the little penguin population.

"It could be a catastrophic wildlife emergency," she said.

"It's very alarming how quickly things are moving.

"Unfortunately, we are likely to see really high mortality rates once this spreads."

Ms Schuringa said not a lot can be done once the birds have contracted the virus.

"The virus is transmitted very quickly and quite easily, so really any area is at risk," she said.

Chris Schuringa says there could be devastating effects on wildlife if the virus reaches Phillip Island. (Supplied)

Ms Schuringa said the virus could spread to other wildlife on the island, such as the island's seal colony and other marine animals.

"It's really only a matter of time before it spreads to other species. Acting now is critical," she said.

Environment Victoria says it wants the state government to strengthen its front line response by restoring funding to key departments who can deal with the crisis, like Parks Victoria, Zoos Victoria and biosecurity staff in the Department of Energy, Environment and Climate Action (DEECA).

Dr Graeme Cooke says community observations help authorities monitor for H5N1. (ABC News)

Vaccination uncertainty

Victoria's chief veterinary officer Graeme Cook said penguin colonies across the world have been very vulnerable to bird flu.

"What we know is that in other parts of the world [mass deaths] have happened," Dr Cook said.

He said trials have shown penguins can be vaccinated without adverse side effects, but could not confirm whether it would be administered before the H5N1 reaches Phillip Island.

"Decisions on whether to vaccinate what we term rare captive and threatened birds has been considered," Dr Cook said.

"But the decision whether to vaccinate is complex.

"There's a decision around risk, there's also the fact that the current vaccine requires that handling to happen twice.

"There's also the fact that in wild bird populations you just can't capture them in the same way that you could, maybe capture captive birds within zoological establishments in order to vaccinate them."

Dr Cook said the federal government ultimately dictated vaccine policy for native species.

Experts are concerned about what could happen to Phillip Island's penguin population. (Supplied: Phillip Island Nature Parks)

Island to stay open

Phillip Island Nature Parks, which overseas the penguin colony, said it was closely monitoring the situation and preparing for the potential arrival of the virus.

"While the disease has not been detected on Phillip Island yet, we have continued our increased monitoring of penguin and seal colonies, and migratory shorebird areas, and have an active Avian Influenza Response Plan in place," a spokesperson said in a statement.

The organisation said its response plan includes increased biosecurity measures for in-field team members such as cleaning and disinfecting footwear and vehicles when moving between sites.

"The Nature Parks has been planning for the arrival of this bird flu strain since 2023, and we continue to work closely with the Department of Energy, Environment and Climate Action (DEECA) on an effective response," the spokesperson said.

The organisation said it has invested significant resources into building the health and resilience of habitat for wildlife on the island in recent years.

Phillip Island Nature Parks attractions, reserves and beaches remain open.

Additional biosecurity measures are being taken to protect the colony of little penguins. (Supplied: Phillip Island Nature Parks)

Another blow for Phillip Island

Bass Coast Shire's mayor Brett Tessari said he hopes wildlife agencies were properly prepared.

"We're relying on the emergency response that's been years in the workings," Cr Tessari said.

"As far as the economic impact goes it will affect us, we're a tourist mecca for penguins."

The arrival of bird flu in Australia is another piece of bad news for the Phillip Island community, which is grappling with the loss of the Australian MotoGP and the World Super Bikes event earlier this year.

"It's just another hit for Phillip Island in particular, we've [lost] the Grand Prix, the World Super Bikes, if our penguins get impacted as well the island's copping it a bit so we're hoping the proper agencies step in and do what they need to do," Cr Tessari said.

World.title: Embattled FIFA boss faces 'blackmail' allegations from ex-staffer
World.content:
Former FIFA vice president Prince Ali bin Al Hussein has criticised the football body's leadership headed by Gianni Infantino, describing prize money withheld from his Jordan national team as a kind of blackmail.

Prince Ali said the Jordanian federation he leads still has not been paid money due for reaching the final of the FIFA Arab Cup played last December in Qatar.

In a social media post, Prince Ali said that during the World Cup — where Jordan made its debut in June — he was told if he endorsed FIFA president Gianni Infantino "it would go a long way to helping our FA out".

Mr Infantino is under pressure to save his 11-year presidency amid a fierce backlash from global football leaders about his now-failed plan to sell a stake in future World Cup profits to investors led by Joshua Kushner.

"We pride ourselves in Jordan in upholding ethical values. We did not endorse him before and certainly will not now," said Prince Ali, who placed third in a five-candidate FIFA presidential contest when Infantino was first elected in February 2016.

"But the whole situation amounts to blackmail, and we refuse to give in to that," the Jordanian royal wrote.

FIFA Arab Cup money not paid

FIFA president Gianni Infantino (left) was on hand to present Morocco the trophy after the Arab Cup final against Jordan last year. (Noushad Thekkayil/NurPhoto via Getty Images)

The 2025 FIFA Arab Cup that Jordan lost in the title match against Morocco was set to pay $4.2 million to the beaten finalist, Jordanian media reported last year.

"The money our team should receive for having reached the final has not been delivered yet," Prince Ali wrote, "while at the same time FIFA brags about how many billions they have in reserve."

"It is clear the problem really is with leadership. For months, FIFA has been refusing to help us on any of these or other matters," he said.

FIFA was approached for comment about the claims.

Prince Ali's FIFA history

Prince Ali Bin Al Hussein (right) and Gianni Infantino (left) look on during a FIFA Congress meeting in 2016. (Getty Images: Matthias Hangst)

Prince Ali was elected by Asian football to serve on FIFA's ruling executive committee from 2011-15, and stood against then-president Sepp Blatter in a May 2015 election. That vote to re-elect Blatter was held in the shadow of raids at Zurich hotels two days earlier to arrest football officials as part of investigations by US and Swiss federal agencies.

Mr Infantino had seemed a lock to be re-elected unopposed for a fourth and final term leading FIFA through 2031 when he left New York two weeks after the World Cup final.

Fallout from his secretive private equity plan revealed one week ago has rocked soccer politics, with Mr Infantino's former colleagues at European football body UEFA now looking for a rival candidate.

The proposal underwritten by Mr Kushner's Thrive Eternal fund would have paid $20 million each to Jordan and all other FIFA members had they accepted by a September 19 deadline

UEFA is also threatening a boycott of FIFA games, events and meetings, while the leadership of the North American soccer body CONCACAF and the Asian Football Confederation, of which Jordan is a member, have also spoken out against Mr Infantino.

FIFA has set a November 18 deadline for candidates to declare for the election by 211 member federations on March 18 in Rabat, Morocco.

World.title: Cream puffs 'deflating for now' as Sydney Chinatown institution shuts
World.content:
Beloved Sydney Chinatown institution Emperor's Garden has shut up shop amid legal action from the Australian Taxation Office, but the restaurant insists it is not all bad news for devotees of its iconic yum cha and takeaway cream puffs.

The popular Haymarket restaurant and bakery has been shuttered with signage noting the premises "has been lawfully re-entered and possession taken" as of Sunday.

The sign — covering 98-100 Hay Street — directs employees to their employer, customers to the restaurant's owners and people who need to recover property to law firm Mills Oakley.

The cream puffs are on pause. (ABC News: Liam Patrick)

Emperor's Garden declined to comment to the ABC, but in a social media post on Monday said: "Our restaurant and bakery are taking a short break. That also means the Puffs are deflating for now.

" We'll be back soon. "

They have been sold for 70 cents each. (ABC News: Millie Roberts)

Mills Oakley, which said it acted for one of the owners of the site, also declined to comment.

Shock closure comes amid redevelopment

There used to be a line of people leading to Emperor's Cream Puff in Chinatown. (ABC News: Liam Patrick)

Emperor's Garden Restaurant has been feeding Sydneysiders since it was opened by Stanley Yee in 1979.

Its takeaway cream puffs, sold from a window for just 70 cents each, have long attracted huge queues of customers looking for a piping hot treat.

The shock closure comes after the Deputy Commissioner of Taxation applied to wind up Emperor's Garden Pty Ltd in early July, with a hearing scheduled in the Federal Court on Friday.

The Emperor's Garden Restaurant pictured in Haymarket in 1987. (Supplied: City of Sydney)

According to the Australian Taxation Office (ATO) website, the enforcement action is taken when a company has failed to pay its debts or it has not been able to negotiate a suitable payment plan.

The City of Sydney council has approved a $44.5 million redevelopment on the site that would allow for internal refurbishments and the construction of a 22-apartment residential tower, taking the premises from three storeys to 16.

"The site is being developed by the long-standing owner-occupiers of the site, who indicate existing food and drink premises within the building will continue to trade post-construction (The Emperors Garden Restaurant and Bakery)," one document said.

Customers have been left confused by the sudden closure. (ABC News: Liam Patrick)

The redevelopment was approved by the council's local planning panel in May subject to a series of conditions, including a detailed environmental site investigation and an amended waste management plan. It has been proposed by Hynsco Pty Ltd.

However, potentially complicating matters, the Deputy Commissioner of Taxation has since applied to wind up Emperor's Garden Pty Ltd with a hearing set down for Friday.

It is not clear what the building's possession and Australian Taxation Office action mean for the redevelopment.

Property records show part of the building is owned by both Hynsco Pty Ltd and M & S Yee while the rest is owned only by Hynsco.

ASIC records show Hynsco is run by Lance and Elaine Lai while M & S Yee refers to Emperor's Garden Pty Ltd directors Stanley and May Ho Yee.

The City of Sydney council approved a $44.5 million redevelopment on the site. (ABC News: Liam Patrick)

Mr Yee's son, Valentine Yee, did not respond to request for comment. Nor did Mr Lai, who is reportedly Mr Yee's nephew.

Emperor's Garden's barbecue noodle site on Thomas Street is still open.

It is not the first matter to rock the Emperor's Garden.

Valentine Yee and brother Jonathan were implicated in a 2022 Independent Commission Against Corruption investigation into Chinese Friends of Labor.

World.title: Engineer says 50 years of erosion research being ignored
World.content:
He might not be a household name, but Angus Gordon played a key role in preserving NSW beaches.

The civil engineer helped develop standards for managing coastal erosion, co-authoring the state's first Coastal Protection Act in 1978, and its revision in 2016.

Coastal engineer Angus Gordon was co-author of the first NSW Coastal Protection Act in 1978, and its revision in 2016. (ABC Central Coast: Keira Proust)

But Mr Gordon said those principles were under threat after the Land and Environment Court ruled beachfront home owners on the NSW Central Coast could build a seawall to protect their properties.

"It seems like nobody took any notice of [the act] and what's happening now is just exactly what I and my colleagues said would happen back in the late 70s," he said.

The Land and Environment Court has granted consent for a 90-metre seawall at The Entrance North. (Supplied: Horton Coastal Engineering)

Mr Gordon said the court decision to allow seawalls at The Entrance North was a "most unfortunate precedent that should never have occurred".

He said he was also disappointed to see Crown Lands sandbagging Byron Bay's Clarkes Beach.

The work is designed to support eroded dunes in front of the state-owned Reflections Holiday Park, but is contrary to his previous recommendation to move structures back from the shoreline and allow nature to run its course.

"Crown Lands should be leading the way as a state government authority," Mr Gordon said.

"But they're not leading the way, they're actually undermining the potential for getting a solution to all this.

"Money is being invested in really silly things, and that's state government money."

Exposed geotechnical bags used to control erosion at Clarkes Beach in Byron Bay. (ABC North Coast Bruce Mackenzie)

A Crown Lands spokesperson said in a statement that a public authority was legally able to install sandbags for a period of up to 90 days.

It said the sandbags already in place in front of the caravan park and the adjacent cafe were approved under development consent from Byron Shire Council until 2037.

A fresh round of sandbagging is expected to start in early August, and Crowns Lands will apply to the Byron Shire Council to allow the new sandbags to stay in place for longer.

In the 1970s, old car bodies were used to prevent sand dune erosion in front of a sand mining site at Belongil in Byron Bay. (Supplied: NSW Public Works)

The current debate is not a new one.

In 1978, Mr Gordon was among a number of experts commissioned by NSW Department of Public Works to produce the Byron Bay-Hastings Point Erosion Study after a "dramatic increase" in coastal erosion problems over the preceding decade.

The report found "individual action to solve site specific problems will not only be ineffective, but it will almost certainly also lead to increasing problems elsewhere".

Mitigation measures such as groynes and sand replenishment were found to offer only short-term solutions, with the authors recommending some areas should be left undeveloped, and gradual retreat planned in others.

The Byron and Tweed Shire councils were urged to control development within 1 kilometre of the shoreline, and stipulate landholders who disregarded the policy did so "at their own risk".

"I've come to the conclusion, after 50 years, that there's very little other option than for the Australian government, Australia-wide, to just simply say, 'You can enjoy the coast while it's there, but property owners cannot protect their property.' End of story," Mr Gordon said.

Residents at Sheltering Palms in northern New South Wales tried to save their homes with rock walls in the 1970s. (Supplied: Angus Gordon)

But for some, living with the fear of watching their homes fall into the ocean, retreat does not seem like a fair option.

Chris Rodgers, president of the Wamberal Protection Association, said it had been fighting to have properties protected from erosion for at least seven years.

"Planned retreat is simply not viable and needs to be taken off the table, as all it does is continue to delay what needs to happen," he said.

Mr Rodgers welcomed the Land & Environment decision and said he hoped the NSW government would now allow all beachfront owners to protect their properties.

Property owners at Wamberal Beach, on the NSW Central Coast are also seeking approval for a permanent structure to prevent any further erosion damage. (ABC Central Coast: Ross McLoughlin)

"Wamberal represents a great opportunity for a buried sandstone protection solution to be introduced and used as a precedent for the rest of NSW," he said.

Mr Rodgers said rock revetment seawalls offered a long-term solution to erosion, that landowners in Wamberal were willing to pay for.

"Seven years after being evacuated and kicked out of our home for two and a half months, and we're still in the same position," he said.

"But we're still fighting for the right thing, and the government just needs to make the right decisions."

Tough discussions

Southern Cross University Deputy Vice-Chancellor of Research, Professor Tim Smith said Australia's legal system was struggling to keep up with coastal property disputes.

The coastal expert's peer-reviewed paper, Beach law in the anthropocene — ScienceDirect, was published in July in the Ocean & Coastal Management journal.

It reviewed legal systems around the world and found private property rights trumped public interest.

"Our common law tradition assumes coastlines are stable and coastal property boundaries can be fixed," Professor Smith said.

"But as the effects of climate change become more dramatic, those assumptions no longer hold."

More sandbags are being installed on Byron Bay's Clarkes Beach to protect properties from erosion. (Bruce MacKenzie: ABC News)

Professor Smith said it was time for tough discussions about a transition strategy.

"We really need to think about what sort of future we want for the coastal zone, and we need to resolve who bears the ultimate rights and responsibilities for these lands — whether we are going to preference private property rights over public rights, whether we're going to preference people's rights over nature's rights," he said.

World.title: Australia news LIVE: Government faces mounting pressure on gambling reforms; Burke delays immigration speech after cabinet meeting
World.content:
Former prime minister Kevin Rudd has said One Nation leader Pauline Hanson is unprepared to do the “hard grinding business of government”, and has no practical responses to the challenges facing Australians.

Former prime minister Kevin Rudd pictured in Sydney last year. Janie Barrett

Speaking on ABC’s 7.30 program last night, Rudd said Hanson’s approach had not changed since she entered politics more than 30 years ago.

“The easy business of politics is simply to act as a protest vector and then lace it and spice it with the politics of race,” he said. “That’s what … Hanson’s been doing ever since she emerged in my fair state of Queensland, a quarter of a century ago. Her script hasn’t changed.”

Rudd, who is now president of the US-based think tank the Asia Society, said Hanson would have no idea how to govern Australia.

“It’s very hard to do the grinding business of government, which looks after practical problems of national security … of the economy and growing it, environmental sustainability … and delivering basic services for the Australian people, including housing affordability, which has been eating away so badly at people’s standard of living over a long period of time.

“Ask this question of yourselves. What single answer does she have to any of the list of problems and challenges which I went through before?”

World.title: ASX set to rise as Wall Street rallies to records; SpaceX posts $768m loss, revenue soars
World.content:
Updated BusinessMarketsWorld markets ASX set to rise as Wall Street rallies to records; SpaceX posts $768m loss, revenue soars Stan Choe Updated August 5, 2026 — 6:50am ,first published 5:17am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The US stock market rallied to records as companies kept piling up profits and oil prices eased. The S&P 500 shot up 1.8 per cent, and the main measure of Wall Street’s health topped its prior all-time high set in June. The Dow Jones Industrial Average added 1.7 per cent to its own record set the day before, and the Nasdaq composite jumped 2.6 per cent. Palantir Technologies and Caterpillar helped lead the way after becoming the latest companies to deliver stronger profits for the spring than expected. Wall Street is roaring higher as a raft of companies deliver better profits for the latest quarter than investors expected. AP The Australian sharemarket is set to rise, with futures at 6.01am AEST pointing to a gain of 35 points, or 0.4 per cent, at the open. The ASX jumped 1.4 per cent to a record high on Tuesday. The Australian dollar is stronger at US70.47¢. SpaceX reported a loss of $US541 million ($767.8 million) in its first quarterly report as a public company, but the loss was less than Wall Street expected and revenue soared.



The company run by Elon Musk, or 9 cents per share, in the three months through June, less than half what financial analysts had expected. Revenue jumped to $US7.8 billion, up more than 90 per cent from the year-earlier period. Despite worries about high inflation, the war in Iran and a possible bubble in stock prices because of euphoria around the boom in artificial-intelligence technology, Wall Street is nearing its latest apex in large part because profits are soaring for companies. Stock prices tend to follow the path of corporate earnings over the long term. Related Article Opinion

Currencies The real reason Trump just rushed to help Japan Stephen Bartholomeusz Senior business columnist Palantir Technologies helped lead the way and soared 29.5 per cent after CEO Alex Karp said its overall revenue leaped 93 per cent in what he called an “otherworldly” quarter. Besides reporting a stronger profit for the spring than analysts expected, the AI company also raised its revenue forecast for the full year of 2026. Caterpillar climbed 5.5 per cent after the heavy-equipment maker likewise reported stronger profit and revenue than analysts expected. It was the first time Caterpillar made more than $US20 billion ($28.4 billion) in sales and revenue in a quarter, and CEO Joe Creed said it’s seeing strong order rates and a growing backlog across its main businesses.



Caterpillar is also benefiting from the AI boom through increased orders for turbines used to power data centres, among other things. They’re the latest companies to deliver even better profits for the latest quarter than investors expected, following strong results from Amazon, Microsoft and others. Coming into this week, companies in the S&P 500 index were on track to deliver growth of nearly 50 per cent in earnings per share for the spring from a year earlier, according to FactSet. That would be the biggest such jump since 2021, when the economy was roaring back to life after cratering in the COVID-19 pandemic. With corporate profits up so much, while stock prices are still roughly where they were two months ago, stocks don’t look as expensive as they did before, according to Phil Segner, a co-portfolio manager at the Leuthold Group. Also helping stocks on Tuesday was another drop for oil prices. Brent crude, the international standard, sank 5.4 per cent to $US79.25 per barrel as hope once again took over from fear in the oil market. It had swung sharply between $US72 and $US102 through July on uncertainty about when the war with Iran would allow oil tankers to freely exit the Persian Gulf again to deliver crude around the world.



It’s jerked up and down many times as uncertainty built, receded and then built again, not only week to week but also hour to hour. Analysts warned more swings could still be ahead, but the latest drop in oil prices nevertheless helped to ease Wall Street’s worries about inflation. That in turn pulled down yields in the bond market, which relaxes pressure on the overall economy and on prices for stocks and other investments. The yield on the 10-year Treasury fell to 4.63 per cent from 4.70 per cent Monday and from 4.75 per cent at the end of last week. That’s a notable move for the bond market, though it remains well above its 3.97 per cent level from before the war with Iran. Higher yields make it more expensive for all kinds of Americans to borrow money, from homebuyers looking for a mortgage to big companies looking to build AI data centres. Related Article Opinion

Appliances He lied about an affair and cost his company nearly $30 million. Now he has a new job Kishor Napier-Raman Senior Business Writer Reports on the US economy, meanwhile, showed it remains resilient even though inflation remains worse than anyone would like. One said US employers were advertising nearly 7.4 million job openings at the end of June, a slight slowdown from May’s level but close to economists’ expectations.



In stock markets abroad, indexes rose modestly across much of Europe and Asia. South Korea’s Kospi had a more significant move and rose 1.6 per cent. Seoul has been home to some of the world’s sharpest swings recently because its stock market is dominated by two companies swept up in AI mania, Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix. The Kospi had dropped 5.1 per cent and soared 17.9 per cent in the prior two days. Stocks of computer chip companies also strengthened on Wall Street, where gains of 2.5 per cent for Nvidia, 6.6 per cent for Broadcom and 7.6 per cent for Micron Technology were some of the strongest forces lifting the S&P 500. World.title: ‘Human safari’: Chilling video of man chased by drone in roadside attack
World.content:
WorldEuropeRussia-Ukraine war ‘Human safari’: Chilling video of man chased by drone in roadside attack David Crowe August 5, 2026 — 5:33am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

London: A man selling vegetables in a Ukrainian town survived an attack by a Russian drone after it chased him around his vehicle in a chilling strike captured on video and shared around the world. The attack drew condemnation as an example of a “human safari” by Russian drone operators who watch for civilians and follow them with their airborne explosives in the manner of a computer game. The video appears to show the market trader being taunted and chased by the Russian drone. X/@ZelenskyyUa Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky described the attack as a crime and said the man under attack in the southern city of Kherson had been wounded in the blast. “A Russian drone deliberately hunted down a man selling vegetables and detonated right next to him,” he said.



“Every single day, ordinary people in Kherson face these Russian ‘safaris’.” Kherson, located across the Dnipro River from Russian forces, has seen hundreds of drone attacks on civilians over the past year, leading local authorities to install netting and other barriers to try to protect citizens. Many of the city’s most important functions have been moved underground to escape the attacks, which became so commonplace that Ukrainians coined the term “human safari” for the Russian tactics. Warning: Graphic content View post on X



The drones are fitted with cameras to allow a “first-person view” by the Russian operator, who can look for a target, even if it is a civilian on a city street. The horrific video highlighted the scale of this threat by showing how the vegetable seller tried to hide from the drone as it hovered around his van. The man was identified as Yurii, 52, who came to Kherson from a nearby area to sell fresh produce, according to the Kyiv Independent and other Ukrainian media. The video shows him trying to dodge the drone, which hovers around and over the van, before the device detonates near him. He was taken to hospital suffering from shrapnel wounds and concussion. In a video released by the local military officials, Yurii said he was trying to show the drone operator that he was only selling vegetables. “But it started flying right at me,” he added. He said his wife was able to escape.



Drone operator is a ‘sadist’ Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha called the attack a “barbaric” Russian war crime and said thousands of similar attacks never reached the public eye. “This is a deliberate and systemic Russian strategy. They know exactly what they are doing. The sadist operating this drone knows full well that he is targeting a civilian,” he said. Drones have increased in speed and range to the point where the danger zone for soldiers and civilians can extend for 25 kilometres on either side of the front line, according to Ukrainian military officials. This “kill zone” is wide enough to include entire cities such as Kherson. When The New York Times reported on the “safaris” in January, local officials said about 200 civilians had been killed and 2000 wounded in the drone strikes over the past year.



Related Article Russia-Ukraine war How dodging drones and death became daily life in eastern Ukraine In May, Ukrainian soldiers in Kherson told a reporter from London’s The Telegraph of the way they hacked into the feeds of the FPV drones to see the vision being relayed to a Russian operator, helping them identify the threats and destroy them. “On a busy day, we might shoot down ten drones,” the operator of the drone detection equipment told the newspaper. One Ukrainian aid worker recently told this masthead of a narrow escape from an FPV drone near a village outside Kharkiv, another city close to Russian forces. “There was an FPV drone just flying after our car, and I was terrified,” said Anastasiia Bilchenko. “We could see, from our drone detector, that the eyes of the drone were following us.”



The Kherson attack came one day after the widespread circulation of a video showing a Ukrainian drone falling on a Russian beach at a Black Sea resort crowded with civilians. Russian officials said seven people died, including three children, and another 58 were injured. Loading The video showed the drone falling at Gelendzhik, east of Crimea, and exploding on the beach. Russian authorities accused Ukraine of targeting civilians, while Ukrainian official Andriy Kovalenko said the drone had been shot down by Russian air defence personnel. World.title: My teenage children want to invest $4000. Where should they start?
World.content:
MoneyInvestingAsk an expert Opinion My teenage children want to invest $4000. Where should they start? Noel Whittaker Money columnist August 5, 2026 — 5:01am

August 5, 2026 — 5:01am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

My children, aged 10 and 13, would like to start investing a modest amount in shares. They will have about $4000 to start and may then top up their investment once or twice a year with birthday, Christmas and pocket money. Could you please outline the best options in terms of simplicity and tax treatment, both now and into the future? I’m not sure whether the shares should be held in my name or theirs. My gross income is about $104,000 and my husband’s is $182,700. We don’t want to spend too much time establishing or maintaining the investment – we’re looking for a “set and forget” approach – but we do want to be able to easily see fees, tax, performance (gains or losses) and overall returns. I’ve heard that platforms such as CommSec and Vanguard are fairly simple. Helping your kids invest their hard-earned can put them well ahead in life. Simon Letch. It’s terrific that your children want to start investing while they’re still so young. Time is the greatest asset an investor has, and starting early can make an enormous difference to the wealth they build over their lifetime. One option is to buy shares or exchange-traded funds (ETFs) through a platform such as CommSec or Vanguard. But before you do that, think carefully about who should own the investment.



If the shares are held in a child’s name, special tax rules apply and investment income above modest limits is generally taxed at penalty rates. If they’re held in a parent’s name, those rules don’t apply, but all income and capital gains are taxed at the parent’s marginal tax rate. There is another option that deserves serious consideration: an investment bond. It’s one of the simplest long-term investments available and ideal for a “set and forget” strategy. The recent changes rushed through Parliament have changed the rules dramatically. An investment bond lets you invest in a range of professionally managed funds while the provider pays the tax internally. That means there’s generally no annual tax return paperwork for you. If you keep the bond for at least 10 years and meet the contribution rules, the proceeds are generally tax-paid when you withdraw them. You can add to the investment each year, making it perfect for birthday and Christmas gifts. Another major advantage is control. You keep ownership of the bond while nominating your child as the beneficiary. That means you decide when they’re mature enough to receive the payment, rather than handing control to them automatically when they reach adulthood.



For families looking for a simple, tax-effective way to build wealth for children or grandchildren, investment bonds are well worth considering. They won’t suit every situation, so it’s worth getting personal financial advice before deciding on the best structure for your family. My father has a share portfolio that originally cost $300,000 and is now worth $500,000. He dies and leaves it to me. If I later leave the portfolio to my daughter in my will, will there be any capital gains tax payable at that time? If not, does she inherit my father’s original cost base? Sadly, no. The recent changes rushed through Parliament have changed the rules dramatically – a death after July 1, 2027, will now trigger a realisation event on any pre-July 1 capital gains. Tax will have to be paid on the capital gain accrued up to June 30, 2027 in the deceased’s date-of-death tax return. The beneficiary then takes the market value at June 30 as their cost base. So, provided your father dies before July 1, 2027, no capital gains tax will be payable on his death, and you will inherit his original cost base of $300,000. But if you then die after July 1, 2027, your estate will have to pay tax on the difference between that $300,000 cost base and the market value at June 30, 2027.



Your daughter will inherit a cost base equal to the market value at June 30, 2027, but unless there are other assets in the estate, some of those shares are likely to have to be sold to pay the tax. That sale will also trigger a separate capital gains tax event on any gain that accrued after July 1, 2027. Editor's pick Opinion

Ask an expert I’m 67 and on the pension. How do I leave my kids a good inheritance? Paul Benson Money contributor I bought a property for $500,000 ten years ago, and its value on June 30, 2027, is $900,000. I sell it two years later for $800,000. Is the $300,000 gain simply treated under the 50 per cent capital gains tax discount, or is there some kind of apportionment? Yes. The post-2027 loss of $100,000 reduces the pre-2027 gain of $400,000. Provided there is nothing else to consider, there is a $300,000 capital gain entitled to the 50 per cent discount. The post-2027 loss reduces the pre-2027 gain before the discount is applied. I am the enduring power of attorney for my 91-year-old aunt, who still has good mental capacity and is actively involved in decisions about her finances. She lives in an Ozcare aged care facility and receives income from two indexed superannuation annuities – her own and one from her late husband. Because of this income, she has paid about $23,000 a year in income tax over the past two financial years. She is expected to reach the lifetime means-tested care fee cap next April, after which more of her income will remain in her account.



She would like to gift $30,000 in cash to family. I know that age pension recipients are generally limited by the gifting rules to $10,000 a year and $30,000 over five years before the deprivation rules apply. However, she is not receiving the age pension. Is she free to gift the full $30,000 without those restrictions? Also, would making the gift reduce the amount of income tax she pays each year? There is no gift tax in Australia, so anybody is free to give away as much money as they wish. The only people who may be affected are those receiving some form of income support. Whether giving away $30,000 would reduce her income tax depends on the assets she is disposing of and the income they are producing. This is something you should discuss with your accountant. Noel Whittaker is author of Retirement Made Simple and other books on personal finance. World.title: Can’t afford a house on your own? This could be the solution
World.content:
MoneyTaxProperty investment Can’t afford a house on your own? This could be the solution Caterina Hrysomallis August 5, 2026 — 5:01am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

When it comes to living with friends, Australians are no strangers, with many of us living in sharehouses in our 20s and 30s. But would you ever take it beyond just renting? A 2024 survey found that over half of Australians would consider buying a property with a friend or sibling. However, only 4 per cent of respondents in the same survey had actually done so. Who says someone should live alone if they don’t want to, just because they’re single? Steven Siewert Current data might reflect otherwise. Deanna Lastrina, senior property lawyer at Nest Legal says, “I’ve had far more enquiries coming in for co-ownership agreements, particularly in the last eight months”. People are wanting “accelerated access into the market, which is particularly hard for first home buyers without parental assistance”.



“You might have lived or grown up in a particular postcode, and perhaps you don’t want to exit that postcode. But by pulling those resources together, you could still live in those ‘untouchable’ areas,” she says. Another big factor? The power of companionship, especially in a post-COVID world. Who says someone should live alone if they don’t want to, just because they’re single? I absolutely believe all friends buying property together should have legal documents drawn up. Deanna Lastrina, senior property lawyer at Nest Legal Karli* and Mark* are a success story. They’re friends who had been renting together for a few years. When they started looking at buying their own homes, Karli realised that if she wanted to stay in a similar area, her budget might only have got her a tiny apartment. The friends started exploring the idea of buying a home together. Four auctions later, they bought a house in May 2024. They’ve been living in the property since.



They’re tenants in common, meaning they have distinct shares in the property and can sell or bequeath as they wish. These shares can be even or uneven. Editor's pick First home buyers I bought a house in my 20s with a friend, and we’re still friends The other structure is a joint tenancy, which involves 50/50 ownership and the “right of survivorship”, meaning if one owner dies, the other automatically inherits the entire property. For friends, Lastrina strongly recommends a tenants in common structure. “Our agreement was a 50/50 split, even if someone else had more money as a deposit,” Karli says. Maintenance and repairs are split 50/50, too. “We did our own research into different banks, as we wanted a loan each and individual offset accounts. Only two banks offered this kind of loan, at the time.” It’s going so well, they’re considering buying an investment property in a regional area.



Lastrina spotlights two big considerations when it comes to these arrangements. “The first is choosing the right person to live with. It goes beyond someone you get along with. They need to be someone that you consider financially disciplined. Someone you’ll be able to resolve conflict with, swiftly.” The second? “I absolutely believe all friends buying property together should have legal documents drawn up.” A “co-ownership agreement” can outline: How much each person initially contributed to the property

How mortgage repayments and bills are paid

How renovations, repayment defaults and disputes are treated

What happens if one owner wants to sell

And what happens if one owner loses decision-making capacity or dies Buyers should also investigate whether they need estate planning and/or family law advice, and to do so at the outset, before the property purchase. One of the biggest mistakes people make is failing to consider worst-case scenarios.



Lastrina recalls one case where two friends bought a property and one sadly passed away. The deceased’s share of the property was passed on to their younger sibling, as per their will. Editor's pick Opinion

Property investment Why Australians can no longer count on property to make them rich “The surviving owner now owns a property with a friend’s younger sibling, a person they don’t really know or trust. Because there was no co-ownership agreement in place, there was no mechanism that meant the surviving owner could easily purchase half of the property.” These agreements aren’t solely about mitigating scenarios as serious. There can be fun clauses, too. “One of my favourite clauses is that every six weeks, the parties have a meeting – almost like an AGM.” Karli and Mark were both single when they bought, which raises the million-dollar question: what happens if one of them enters a relationship?



“Ideally, the plan would be to rent the property out rather than add a third person into the considerations.” They’ve decided to discuss this further if the time comes and re-engage a lawyer. Lastrina says that people can stipulate what happens if an owner finds a partner in a co-ownership agreement. If this does happen, she recommends the couple sets up a binding financial agreement (Australia’s version of a prenup) giving them more certainty around how their respective interests would be dealt with if they separated, which can indirectly benefit co-owners by providing greater clarity in the event of relationship breakdowns. *These names have been changed. World.title: Think soup is boring? These bowls bring colour, crunch and main meal energy
World.content:
From halloumi fries to crispy-skinned chicken, these hearty soups have the satisfying texture already built in. No side of bread required.

I love soup. But I know sceptics exist. To them, soup isn’t a meal unless it’s accompanied by a cheese-oozing toastie or a slab of sourdough the size of a world atlas.

Honestly? I respect that kind of aggressive dedication to dinner. But to save you the side-dish admin, I’ve skipped straight to the chase. Here are soups with the something-something already built in. We’re talking halloumi fries, dunkable spring rolls and hunks of gloriously crispy-skinned chicken. No sides required.

Halloumi “fries” launch zaatar-roasted tomato soup into a new flavour realm. Katrina Meynink

Zaatar-roasted tomato soup with halloumi fries

In culinary school, a German chef once admonished my “thick soup”, going on a tirade about Australians and our horrifying love for a dense puree. Consider me a proud, card-carrying thick-soup advocate until the end of my days. How else could a bowl carry the piping hot, salty squeak of tanned halloumi fries? It takes a standard tomato soup and pushes it into an entirely new realm of mealtime.

World.title: Legendary hotel’s revamp gets it a perfect score
World.content:
Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The hotel: Villa San Michele, Fiesole, Florence Check-in Villa San Michele has a serene setting, high in the hills above Florence. Jonangelo Molinari After navigating a chaotic Florence airport and some hairy hairpin bends in our hire-car, arriving at this newly renovated Renaissance villa – its facade attributed to the school of Michelangelo – feels even more like a serene escape from life’s mundane realities. Architect and designer Luigi Fragola says it was the stillness of the villa that first struck him as he walked through the 15th-century estate: “What fascinated me was the silence – that silence of places that have truly lived.” The terraced gardens at Villa San Michele. Mattia Aquila Formerly a convent, at one time Napoleon’s headquarters and more recently a private home, the building, set high in the Fiesole hills above Tuscany’s capital, has been painstakingly reimagined. It’s also now the hotel du jour for the rich and fabulous (model Alexa Chung and DJ Isabella Massenet were at the reopening party). Given the Lamborghini, Porsche and Ferrari in the driveway, I’m also somewhat relieved we were upgraded to a Mercedes instead of the Opel Astra I’d booked online. 



Interior of the Villa San Michele. The villa is set in cascading botanical gardens designed by landscape architect Pietro Porcinai. Adrian Gaut While original cloisters, stone fireplaces, restored frescoes and heavy curtains speak to its weighty history, works by Italian artists – hand-painted murals by Francesca Guicciardini, watercolours by botanical artist Maria Rita Stirpe, wall coverings by Elena Carozzi – bring present-day personality. The terraced gardens, with 180-degree views as far as Brunelleschi’s cupola crowning the Duomo, are a highlight: lavender and rosemary scent the gravel pathways, while the lemon trees are the healthiest I’ve seen, weighed down with enormous fruit. The room A garden suite features artisan furniture and beautiful textiles. Adrian Gaut Bathrooms are luxurious, with green marble and Acqua di Parma toiletries. Adrian Gaut We’re staying in a garden suite that’s seemingly built into the hillside, jasmine hedges camouflaging our private alfresco area from passers-by. There are, of course, rooms in the villa itself (39 altogether), but being enveloped in nature feels wonderfully therapeutic. The green Cipollino marble in the bathroom and local Impruneta terracotta floors echo the gardens outside, while raw linens and a chalky palette reflect Fragola’s restrained approach. Artisanal details include hand-painted tapestries, silks from Venice-based Rubelli and ornate scagliola [a 17th-century plastering technique] tabletops by Tuscan workshop Bianco Bianchi.



Food + drink An original cloister houses the lounge area. Adrian Gaut It’s appropriate that a fresco of The Last Supper adorns the original refectory where a sumptuous buffet breakfast is laid out – there are so many irresistible cakes and pastries alongside cured meats, cheese, yoghurt, juices, fruit and yes, eight types of honey (the villa has its own beehives), that you need never eat again. And that’s without ordering eggs Florentine from the a la carte menu. Under a striped awning at the alfresco pool grill, try a vibrant Caprese salad or linguine alla Nerano (with zucchini); at Ristorante San Michele it’s all about the caponata, the eggplant parmigiana and the Chianina beef used in the tartare. The sheer volume of local and seasonal ingredients is impressive. Dishes get more intricate at Antesi, the eight-table fine dining restaurant in the 16th-century loggia, where executive chef Alessandro Cozzolino conjures an ambitious culinary journey called the “cuisine of time” – the elaborate presentation occasionally taking precedence over depth of flavour. The intimate Bar Doccia is your spot for aperitivi. Jonangelo Molinari For a more casual experience, the intimate Bar Doccia offers an excellent drinks list including several non-alcoholic aperitivi, alongside substantial snacks. As is traditional, if you order a couple of cocktails you’ll also be served bowls of olives, almonds and chips but maybe treat yourself to a couple of croquettes blanketed in shaved white truffle for good measure.



Out and about The view from the Garden Junior Suite. Adrian Gaut You don’t have to travel far to dip into the area’s history: nearby Monte Ceceri is where Leonardo da Vinci came to study local birds of prey and eventually tested his “great kite” flying machine. The hotel offers several immersive experiences including a hike through those woodlands, a calligraphy masterclass and a paper-making workshop, while its shuttle bus will drop you in the centre of Florence at Piazza della Repubblica (so much easier than attempting Fiesole’s narrow, winding roads yourself). Wellness devotees are also looked after, with three treatment rooms including a double suite at Italy’s first Guerlain spa, and, up in the woods, an Energy Chapel, Sungazing Lounge and yoga deck designed by super-cool Milanese lifestyle brand La DoubleJ. Villa San Michele’s swimming pool. Letizia Cigliutti The verdict The celebration of Italian craftsmanship and the level of thoughtful detail at this historic Franciscan convent, combined with the sublime peace of its gardens, make a stay here unforgettable. Essentials

World.title: I’m a breastfeeding mum. How much should my workplace cater to me?
World.content:
LifestyleLife & relationshipsGot a Minute? I’m a breastfeeding mum. How much should my workplace cater to me? Kirstin Ferguson August 5, 2026 — 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Each week Dr Kirstin Ferguson tackles questions about workplace, career and leadership in her advice column Got a Minute? This week: a missing office after maternity leave, bogus corporate values and bring forced to take leave. The best employers welcome people back from maternity and paternity leave. Dionne Gain I’m on maternity leave, returning to work in two months. While I’ve been away, my private office has been reassigned (I now need to hot-desk) and I’ve been told I’ll need to work from a different building two days a week. Before going on leave, my employer and I agreed I could use my office to express milk when I returned, but that office is no longer mine. HR is trying to find an alternative solution but nothing is confirmed, and the options suggested so far include booking a boardroom some distance away, or using a parents’ room in an entirely different building. These feel impractical for someone who needs to express multiple times a day. Is any of this reasonable? Just because you took parental leave does not mean you should be expected to accept reduced working conditions. The best employers welcome people back from maternity and paternity leave, rather than making them feel like an imposition.



Related Article Got a Minute? My holiday was ruined by a redundancy threat. I stayed, but I’m still mad Your employer has specific legal obligations regarding breastfeeding, which is a protected ground of discrimination. The failure to provide adequate facilities may be a breach of work health and safety laws. You should request a private room with a comfortable chair, a fridge where you can store breast milk and somewhere to store your breast pump. It is difficult to see how booking out the boardroom, for example, would meet those requirements. Rather than debating the loss of your office itself, keep the discussion focused on outcomes. Explain why the proposed alternatives won’t work in practice and ask HR to work with you on a solution that is private, close and consistently available. If that doesn’t happen, you might like to seek advice from the Australian Human Rights Commission about your rights.



I work in an investment bank that has a set of values, including a “speak up” culture. However, the reality is the opposite. When issues – with evidence – were raised about a senior female executive of undermining behaviour and bullying, they were shut down by HR. This female executive has had many complaints about her behaviour; however, she continues to behave poorly, lies and manipulates her boss. Our team has suffered much turnover due to her inappropriate behaviour. How would you approach this situation? It is easy to list a bunch of values and stick them on a wall. It is much harder to actually live them. In any organisation, if values are not being lived “from the top”, the chances are the values are unlikely to be lived at all. If complaints about this woman have been repeatedly ignored despite evidence, the issue is no longer one difficult executive but a leadership culture that tolerates the behaviour. That doesn’t mean you should stop raising concerns, but be strategic. Keep records, stick to facts rather than opinions, and use whatever formal reporting channels are available. If nothing changes, consider whether you think things will ever really change. If the answer is no, sometimes the only thing you can do is send a message by taking your talents and loyalty somewhere else. My workplace has a lot of long-term staff who are constantly being pushed to take their long service leave. I understand companies do not want the high liabilities on their balance sheet, but employees feel like they are being forced to take leave when they do not want to. Are there any laws around this? Can a company legally force you to take it?



Related Article Got a Minute? My bad date is threatening to go to my employer. How can I stop her? The first thing employers need to remember is that long service leave is an entitlement, not just some sort of balance sheet problem to be dealt with. There is a big difference between encouraging someone to take their long service leave, and forcing someone to take it (the “use it or lose it” idea). While employers can sometimes direct employees to take long service leave, the rules vary between states and territories and will often depend on the circumstances. If your employer is forcing people to take leave, you can ask what policy or legal basis they’re relying on. You can check the specific long service leave rules that apply where you work by seeking advice from your union, HR or the Fair Work Ombudsman. To submit a question about work, careers or leadership, visit kirstinferguson.com/ask. You will not be asked to provide your name or any identifying information. Letters may be edited. World.title: Australia news LIVE: Government faces mounting pressure on gambling reforms; Burke delays immigration speech after cabinet meeting
World.content:
Former prime minister Kevin Rudd has said One Nation leader Pauline Hanson is unprepared to do the “hard grinding business of government”, and has no practical responses to the challenges facing Australians.

Former prime minister Kevin Rudd pictured in Sydney last year. Janie Barrett

Speaking on ABC’s 7.30 program last night, Rudd said Hanson’s approach had not changed since she entered politics more than 30 years ago.

“The easy business of politics is simply to act as a protest vector and then lace it and spice it with the politics of race,” he said. “That’s what … Hanson’s been doing ever since she emerged in my fair state of Queensland, a quarter of a century ago. Her script hasn’t changed.”

Rudd, who is now president of the US-based think tank the Asia Society, said Hanson would have no idea how to govern Australia.

“It’s very hard to do the grinding business of government, which looks after practical problems of national security … of the economy and growing it, environmental sustainability … and delivering basic services for the Australian people, including housing affordability, which has been eating away so badly at people’s standard of living over a long period of time.

“Ask this question of yourselves. What single answer does she have to any of the list of problems and challenges which I went through before?”

World.title: ASX set to rise as Wall Street rallies to records; SpaceX posts $768m loss, revenue soars
World.content:
Updated BusinessMarketsWorld markets ASX set to rise as Wall Street rallies to records; SpaceX posts $768m loss, revenue soars Stan Choe Updated August 5, 2026 — 6:50am ,first published 5:17am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The US stock market rallied to records as companies kept piling up profits and oil prices eased. The S&P 500 shot up 1.8 per cent, and the main measure of Wall Street’s health topped its prior all-time high set in June. The Dow Jones Industrial Average added 1.7 per cent to its own record set the day before, and the Nasdaq composite jumped 2.6 per cent. Palantir Technologies and Caterpillar helped lead the way after becoming the latest companies to deliver stronger profits for the spring than expected. Wall Street is roaring higher as a raft of companies deliver better profits for the latest quarter than investors expected. AP The Australian sharemarket is set to rise, with futures at 6.01am AEST pointing to a gain of 35 points, or 0.4 per cent, at the open. The ASX jumped 1.4 per cent to a record high on Tuesday. The Australian dollar is stronger at US70.47¢. SpaceX reported a loss of $US541 million ($767.8 million) in its first quarterly report as a public company, but the loss was less than Wall Street expected and revenue soared.



The company run by Elon Musk, or 9 cents per share, in the three months through June, less than half what financial analysts had expected. Revenue jumped to $US7.8 billion, up more than 90 per cent from the year-earlier period. Despite worries about high inflation, the war in Iran and a possible bubble in stock prices because of euphoria around the boom in artificial-intelligence technology, Wall Street is nearing its latest apex in large part because profits are soaring for companies. Stock prices tend to follow the path of corporate earnings over the long term. Related Article Opinion

Currencies The real reason Trump just rushed to help Japan Stephen Bartholomeusz Senior business columnist Palantir Technologies helped lead the way and soared 29.5 per cent after CEO Alex Karp said its overall revenue leaped 93 per cent in what he called an “otherworldly” quarter. Besides reporting a stronger profit for the spring than analysts expected, the AI company also raised its revenue forecast for the full year of 2026. Caterpillar climbed 5.5 per cent after the heavy-equipment maker likewise reported stronger profit and revenue than analysts expected. It was the first time Caterpillar made more than $US20 billion ($28.4 billion) in sales and revenue in a quarter, and CEO Joe Creed said it’s seeing strong order rates and a growing backlog across its main businesses.



Caterpillar is also benefiting from the AI boom through increased orders for turbines used to power data centres, among other things. They’re the latest companies to deliver even better profits for the latest quarter than investors expected, following strong results from Amazon, Microsoft and others. Coming into this week, companies in the S&P 500 index were on track to deliver growth of nearly 50 per cent in earnings per share for the spring from a year earlier, according to FactSet. That would be the biggest such jump since 2021, when the economy was roaring back to life after cratering in the COVID-19 pandemic. With corporate profits up so much, while stock prices are still roughly where they were two months ago, stocks don’t look as expensive as they did before, according to Phil Segner, a co-portfolio manager at the Leuthold Group. Also helping stocks on Tuesday was another drop for oil prices. Brent crude, the international standard, sank 5.4 per cent to $US79.25 per barrel as hope once again took over from fear in the oil market. It had swung sharply between $US72 and $US102 through July on uncertainty about when the war with Iran would allow oil tankers to freely exit the Persian Gulf again to deliver crude around the world.



It’s jerked up and down many times as uncertainty built, receded and then built again, not only week to week but also hour to hour. Analysts warned more swings could still be ahead, but the latest drop in oil prices nevertheless helped to ease Wall Street’s worries about inflation. That in turn pulled down yields in the bond market, which relaxes pressure on the overall economy and on prices for stocks and other investments. The yield on the 10-year Treasury fell to 4.63 per cent from 4.70 per cent Monday and from 4.75 per cent at the end of last week. That’s a notable move for the bond market, though it remains well above its 3.97 per cent level from before the war with Iran. Higher yields make it more expensive for all kinds of Americans to borrow money, from homebuyers looking for a mortgage to big companies looking to build AI data centres. Related Article Opinion

Appliances He lied about an affair and cost his company nearly $30 million. Now he has a new job Kishor Napier-Raman Senior Business Writer Reports on the US economy, meanwhile, showed it remains resilient even though inflation remains worse than anyone would like. One said US employers were advertising nearly 7.4 million job openings at the end of June, a slight slowdown from May’s level but close to economists’ expectations.



In stock markets abroad, indexes rose modestly across much of Europe and Asia. South Korea’s Kospi had a more significant move and rose 1.6 per cent. Seoul has been home to some of the world’s sharpest swings recently because its stock market is dominated by two companies swept up in AI mania, Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix. The Kospi had dropped 5.1 per cent and soared 17.9 per cent in the prior two days. Stocks of computer chip companies also strengthened on Wall Street, where gains of 2.5 per cent for Nvidia, 6.6 per cent for Broadcom and 7.6 per cent for Micron Technology were some of the strongest forces lifting the S&P 500. World.title: ‘Human safari’: Chilling video of man chased by drone in roadside attack
World.content:
WorldEuropeRussia-Ukraine war ‘Human safari’: Chilling video of man chased by drone in roadside attack David Crowe August 5, 2026 — 5:33am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

London: A man selling vegetables in a Ukrainian town survived an attack by a Russian drone after it chased him around his vehicle in a chilling strike captured on video and shared around the world. The attack drew condemnation as an example of a “human safari” by Russian drone operators who watch for civilians and follow them with their airborne explosives in the manner of a computer game. The video appears to show the market trader being taunted and chased by the Russian drone. X/@ZelenskyyUa Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky described the attack as a crime and said the man under attack in the southern city of Kherson had been wounded in the blast. “A Russian drone deliberately hunted down a man selling vegetables and detonated right next to him,” he said.



“Every single day, ordinary people in Kherson face these Russian ‘safaris’.” Kherson, located across the Dnipro River from Russian forces, has seen hundreds of drone attacks on civilians over the past year, leading local authorities to install netting and other barriers to try to protect citizens. Many of the city’s most important functions have been moved underground to escape the attacks, which became so commonplace that Ukrainians coined the term “human safari” for the Russian tactics. Warning: Graphic content View post on X



The drones are fitted with cameras to allow a “first-person view” by the Russian operator, who can look for a target, even if it is a civilian on a city street. The horrific video highlighted the scale of this threat by showing how the vegetable seller tried to hide from the drone as it hovered around his van. The man was identified as Yurii, 52, who came to Kherson from a nearby area to sell fresh produce, according to the Kyiv Independent and other Ukrainian media. The video shows him trying to dodge the drone, which hovers around and over the van, before the device detonates near him. He was taken to hospital suffering from shrapnel wounds and concussion. In a video released by the local military officials, Yurii said he was trying to show the drone operator that he was only selling vegetables. “But it started flying right at me,” he added. He said his wife was able to escape.



Drone operator is a ‘sadist’ Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha called the attack a “barbaric” Russian war crime and said thousands of similar attacks never reached the public eye. “This is a deliberate and systemic Russian strategy. They know exactly what they are doing. The sadist operating this drone knows full well that he is targeting a civilian,” he said. Drones have increased in speed and range to the point where the danger zone for soldiers and civilians can extend for 25 kilometres on either side of the front line, according to Ukrainian military officials. This “kill zone” is wide enough to include entire cities such as Kherson. When The New York Times reported on the “safaris” in January, local officials said about 200 civilians had been killed and 2000 wounded in the drone strikes over the past year.



Related Article Russia-Ukraine war How dodging drones and death became daily life in eastern Ukraine In May, Ukrainian soldiers in Kherson told a reporter from London’s The Telegraph of the way they hacked into the feeds of the FPV drones to see the vision being relayed to a Russian operator, helping them identify the threats and destroy them. “On a busy day, we might shoot down ten drones,” the operator of the drone detection equipment told the newspaper. One Ukrainian aid worker recently told this masthead of a narrow escape from an FPV drone near a village outside Kharkiv, another city close to Russian forces. “There was an FPV drone just flying after our car, and I was terrified,” said Anastasiia Bilchenko. “We could see, from our drone detector, that the eyes of the drone were following us.”



The Kherson attack came one day after the widespread circulation of a video showing a Ukrainian drone falling on a Russian beach at a Black Sea resort crowded with civilians. Russian officials said seven people died, including three children, and another 58 were injured. Loading The video showed the drone falling at Gelendzhik, east of Crimea, and exploding on the beach. Russian authorities accused Ukraine of targeting civilians, while Ukrainian official Andriy Kovalenko said the drone had been shot down by Russian air defence personnel.
