World.title: My teenage children want to invest $4000. Where should they start?
World.content:
MoneyInvestingAsk an expert Opinion My teenage children want to invest $4000. Where should they start? Noel Whittaker Money columnist August 5, 2026 — 5:01am

August 5, 2026 — 5:01am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

My children, aged 10 and 13, would like to start investing a modest amount in shares. They will have about $4000 to start and may then top up their investment once or twice a year with birthday, Christmas and pocket money. Could you please outline the best options in terms of simplicity and tax treatment, both now and into the future? I’m not sure whether the shares should be held in my name or theirs. My gross income is about $104,000 and my husband’s is $182,700. We don’t want to spend too much time establishing or maintaining the investment – we’re looking for a “set and forget” approach – but we do want to be able to easily see fees, tax, performance (gains or losses) and overall returns. I’ve heard that platforms such as CommSec and Vanguard are fairly simple. Helping your kids invest their hard-earned can put them well ahead in life. Simon Letch. It’s terrific that your children want to start investing while they’re still so young. Time is the greatest asset an investor has, and starting early can make an enormous difference to the wealth they build over their lifetime. One option is to buy shares or exchange-traded funds (ETFs) through a platform such as CommSec or Vanguard. But before you do that, think carefully about who should own the investment.



If the shares are held in a child’s name, special tax rules apply and investment income above modest limits is generally taxed at penalty rates. If they’re held in a parent’s name, those rules don’t apply, but all income and capital gains are taxed at the parent’s marginal tax rate. There is another option that deserves serious consideration: an investment bond. It’s one of the simplest long-term investments available and ideal for a “set and forget” strategy. The recent changes rushed through Parliament have changed the rules dramatically. An investment bond lets you invest in a range of professionally managed funds while the provider pays the tax internally. That means there’s generally no annual tax return paperwork for you. If you keep the bond for at least 10 years and meet the contribution rules, the proceeds are generally tax-paid when you withdraw them. You can add to the investment each year, making it perfect for birthday and Christmas gifts. Another major advantage is control. You keep ownership of the bond while nominating your child as the beneficiary. That means you decide when they’re mature enough to receive the payment, rather than handing control to them automatically when they reach adulthood.



For families looking for a simple, tax-effective way to build wealth for children or grandchildren, investment bonds are well worth considering. They won’t suit every situation, so it’s worth getting personal financial advice before deciding on the best structure for your family. My father has a share portfolio that originally cost $300,000 and is now worth $500,000. He dies and leaves it to me. If I later leave the portfolio to my daughter in my will, will there be any capital gains tax payable at that time? If not, does she inherit my father’s original cost base? Sadly, no. The recent changes rushed through Parliament have changed the rules dramatically – a death after July 1, 2027, will now trigger a realisation event on any pre-July 1 capital gains. Tax will have to be paid on the capital gain accrued up to June 30, 2027 in the deceased’s date-of-death tax return. The beneficiary then takes the market value at June 30 as their cost base. So, provided your father dies before July 1, 2027, no capital gains tax will be payable on his death, and you will inherit his original cost base of $300,000. But if you then die after July 1, 2027, your estate will have to pay tax on the difference between that $300,000 cost base and the market value at June 30, 2027.



Your daughter will inherit a cost base equal to the market value at June 30, 2027, but unless there are other assets in the estate, some of those shares are likely to have to be sold to pay the tax. That sale will also trigger a separate capital gains tax event on any gain that accrued after July 1, 2027. Editor's pick Opinion

Ask an expert I’m 67 and on the pension. How do I leave my kids a good inheritance? Paul Benson Money contributor I bought a property for $500,000 ten years ago, and its value on June 30, 2027, is $900,000. I sell it two years later for $800,000. Is the $300,000 gain simply treated under the 50 per cent capital gains tax discount, or is there some kind of apportionment? Yes. The post-2027 loss of $100,000 reduces the pre-2027 gain of $400,000. Provided there is nothing else to consider, there is a $300,000 capital gain entitled to the 50 per cent discount. The post-2027 loss reduces the pre-2027 gain before the discount is applied. I am the enduring power of attorney for my 91-year-old aunt, who still has good mental capacity and is actively involved in decisions about her finances. She lives in an Ozcare aged care facility and receives income from two indexed superannuation annuities – her own and one from her late husband. Because of this income, she has paid about $23,000 a year in income tax over the past two financial years. She is expected to reach the lifetime means-tested care fee cap next April, after which more of her income will remain in her account.



She would like to gift $30,000 in cash to family. I know that age pension recipients are generally limited by the gifting rules to $10,000 a year and $30,000 over five years before the deprivation rules apply. However, she is not receiving the age pension. Is she free to gift the full $30,000 without those restrictions? Also, would making the gift reduce the amount of income tax she pays each year? There is no gift tax in Australia, so anybody is free to give away as much money as they wish. The only people who may be affected are those receiving some form of income support. Whether giving away $30,000 would reduce her income tax depends on the assets she is disposing of and the income they are producing. This is something you should discuss with your accountant. Noel Whittaker is author of Retirement Made Simple and other books on personal finance. Questions to: noel@noelwhittaker.com.au Advice given in this article is general in nature and is not intended to influence readers’ decisions about investing or financial products. They should always seek their own professional advice that takes into account their own personal circumstances before making any financial decisions. World.title: Can’t afford a house on your own? This could be the solution
World.content:
MoneyTaxProperty investment Can’t afford a house on your own? This could be the solution Caterina Hrysomallis August 5, 2026 — 5:01am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

When it comes to living with friends, Australians are no strangers, with many of us living in sharehouses in our 20s and 30s. But would you ever take it beyond just renting? A 2024 survey found that over half of Australians would consider buying a property with a friend or sibling. However, only 4 per cent of respondents in the same survey had actually done so. Who says someone should live alone if they don’t want to, just because they’re single? Steven Siewert Current data might reflect otherwise. Deanna Lastrina, senior property lawyer at Nest Legal says, “I’ve had far more enquiries coming in for co-ownership agreements, particularly in the last eight months”. People are wanting “accelerated access into the market, which is particularly hard for first home buyers without parental assistance”.



“You might have lived or grown up in a particular postcode, and perhaps you don’t want to exit that postcode. But by pulling those resources together, you could still live in those ‘untouchable’ areas,” she says. Another big factor? The power of companionship, especially in a post-COVID world. Who says someone should live alone if they don’t want to, just because they’re single? I absolutely believe all friends buying property together should have legal documents drawn up. Deanna Lastrina, senior property lawyer at Nest Legal Karli* and Mark* are a success story. They’re friends who had been renting together for a few years. When they started looking at buying their own homes, Karli realised that if she wanted to stay in a similar area, her budget might only have got her a tiny apartment. The friends started exploring the idea of buying a home together. Four auctions later, they bought a house in May 2024. They’ve been living in the property since.



They’re tenants in common, meaning they have distinct shares in the property and can sell or bequeath as they wish. These shares can be even or uneven. Editor's pick First home buyers I bought a house in my 20s with a friend, and we’re still friends The other structure is a joint tenancy, which involves 50/50 ownership and the “right of survivorship”, meaning if one owner dies, the other automatically inherits the entire property. For friends, Lastrina strongly recommends a tenants in common structure. “Our agreement was a 50/50 split, even if someone else had more money as a deposit,” Karli says. Maintenance and repairs are split 50/50, too. “We did our own research into different banks, as we wanted a loan each and individual offset accounts. Only two banks offered this kind of loan, at the time.” It’s going so well, they’re considering buying an investment property in a regional area.



Lastrina spotlights two big considerations when it comes to these arrangements. “The first is choosing the right person to live with. It goes beyond someone you get along with. They need to be someone that you consider financially disciplined. Someone you’ll be able to resolve conflict with, swiftly.” The second? “I absolutely believe all friends buying property together should have legal documents drawn up.” A “co-ownership agreement” can outline: How much each person initially contributed to the property

How mortgage repayments and bills are paid

How renovations, repayment defaults and disputes are treated

What happens if one owner wants to sell

And what happens if one owner loses decision-making capacity or dies Buyers should also investigate whether they need estate planning and/or family law advice, and to do so at the outset, before the property purchase. One of the biggest mistakes people make is failing to consider worst-case scenarios.



Lastrina recalls one case where two friends bought a property and one sadly passed away. The deceased’s share of the property was passed on to their younger sibling, as per their will. Editor's pick Opinion

Property investment Why Australians can no longer count on property to make them rich “The surviving owner now owns a property with a friend’s younger sibling, a person they don’t really know or trust. Because there was no co-ownership agreement in place, there was no mechanism that meant the surviving owner could easily purchase half of the property.” These agreements aren’t solely about mitigating scenarios as serious. There can be fun clauses, too. “One of my favourite clauses is that every six weeks, the parties have a meeting – almost like an AGM.” Karli and Mark were both single when they bought, which raises the million-dollar question: what happens if one of them enters a relationship?



“Ideally, the plan would be to rent the property out rather than add a third person into the considerations.” They’ve decided to discuss this further if the time comes and re-engage a lawyer. Lastrina says that people can stipulate what happens if an owner finds a partner in a co-ownership agreement. If this does happen, she recommends the couple sets up a binding financial agreement (Australia’s version of a prenup) giving them more certainty around how their respective interests would be dealt with if they separated, which can indirectly benefit co-owners by providing greater clarity in the event of relationship breakdowns. *These names have been changed. Advice given in this article is general in nature and is not intended to influence readers’ decisions about investing or financial products. They should always seek their own professional advice that takes into account their personal circumstances before making any financial decisions. World.title: Think soup is boring? These bowls bring colour, crunch and main meal energy
World.content:
From halloumi fries to crispy-skinned chicken, these hearty soups have the satisfying texture already built in. No side of bread required.

I love soup. But I know sceptics exist. To them, soup isn’t a meal unless it’s accompanied by a cheese-oozing toastie or a slab of sourdough the size of a world atlas.

Honestly? I respect that kind of aggressive dedication to dinner. But to save you the side-dish admin, I’ve skipped straight to the chase. Here are soups with the something-something already built in. We’re talking halloumi fries, dunkable spring rolls and hunks of gloriously crispy-skinned chicken. No sides required.

Halloumi “fries” launch zaatar-roasted tomato soup into a new flavour realm. Katrina Meynink

Zaatar-roasted tomato soup with halloumi fries

In culinary school, a German chef once admonished my “thick soup”, going on a tirade about Australians and our horrifying love for a dense puree. Consider me a proud, card-carrying thick-soup advocate until the end of my days. How else could a bowl carry the piping hot, salty squeak of tanned halloumi fries? It takes a standard tomato soup and pushes it into an entirely new realm of mealtime.

World.title: Legendary hotel’s revamp gets it a perfect score
World.content:
Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The hotel: Villa San Michele, Fiesole, Florence Check-in Villa San Michele has a serene setting, high in the hills above Florence. Jonangelo Molinari After navigating a chaotic Florence airport and some hairy hairpin bends in our hire-car, arriving at this newly renovated Renaissance villa – its facade attributed to the school of Michelangelo – feels even more like a serene escape from life’s mundane realities. Architect and designer Luigi Fragola says it was the stillness of the villa that first struck him as he walked through the 15th-century estate: “What fascinated me was the silence – that silence of places that have truly lived.” The terraced gardens at Villa San Michele. Mattia Aquila Formerly a convent, at one time Napoleon’s headquarters and more recently a private home, the building, set high in the Fiesole hills above Tuscany’s capital, has been painstakingly reimagined. It’s also now the hotel du jour for the rich and fabulous (model Alexa Chung and DJ Isabella Massenet were at the reopening party). Given the Lamborghini, Porsche and Ferrari in the driveway, I’m also somewhat relieved we were upgraded to a Mercedes instead of the Opel Astra I’d booked online. 



Interior of the Villa San Michele. The villa is set in cascading botanical gardens designed by landscape architect Pietro Porcinai. Adrian Gaut While original cloisters, stone fireplaces, restored frescoes and heavy curtains speak to its weighty history, works by Italian artists – hand-painted murals by Francesca Guicciardini, watercolours by botanical artist Maria Rita Stirpe, wall coverings by Elena Carozzi – bring present-day personality. The terraced gardens, with 180-degree views as far as Brunelleschi’s cupola crowning the Duomo, are a highlight: lavender and rosemary scent the gravel pathways, while the lemon trees are the healthiest I’ve seen, weighed down with enormous fruit. The room A garden suite features artisan furniture and beautiful textiles. Adrian Gaut Bathrooms are luxurious, with green marble and Acqua di Parma toiletries. Adrian Gaut We’re staying in a garden suite that’s seemingly built into the hillside, jasmine hedges camouflaging our private alfresco area from passers-by. There are, of course, rooms in the villa itself (39 altogether), but being enveloped in nature feels wonderfully therapeutic. The green Cipollino marble in the bathroom and local Impruneta terracotta floors echo the gardens outside, while raw linens and a chalky palette reflect Fragola’s restrained approach. Artisanal details include hand-painted tapestries, silks from Venice-based Rubelli and ornate scagliola [a 17th-century plastering technique] tabletops by Tuscan workshop Bianco Bianchi.



Food + drink An original cloister houses the lounge area. Adrian Gaut It’s appropriate that a fresco of The Last Supper adorns the original refectory where a sumptuous buffet breakfast is laid out – there are so many irresistible cakes and pastries alongside cured meats, cheese, yoghurt, juices, fruit and yes, eight types of honey (the villa has its own beehives), that you need never eat again. And that’s without ordering eggs Florentine from the a la carte menu. Under a striped awning at the alfresco pool grill, try a vibrant Caprese salad or linguine alla Nerano (with zucchini); at Ristorante San Michele it’s all about the caponata, the eggplant parmigiana and the Chianina beef used in the tartare. The sheer volume of local and seasonal ingredients is impressive. Dishes get more intricate at Antesi, the eight-table fine dining restaurant in the 16th-century loggia, where executive chef Alessandro Cozzolino conjures an ambitious culinary journey called the “cuisine of time” – the elaborate presentation occasionally taking precedence over depth of flavour. The intimate Bar Doccia is your spot for aperitivi. Jonangelo Molinari For a more casual experience, the intimate Bar Doccia offers an excellent drinks list including several non-alcoholic aperitivi, alongside substantial snacks. As is traditional, if you order a couple of cocktails you’ll also be served bowls of olives, almonds and chips but maybe treat yourself to a couple of croquettes blanketed in shaved white truffle for good measure.



Out and about The view from the Garden Junior Suite. Adrian Gaut You don’t have to travel far to dip into the area’s history: nearby Monte Ceceri is where Leonardo da Vinci came to study local birds of prey and eventually tested his “great kite” flying machine. The hotel offers several immersive experiences including a hike through those woodlands, a calligraphy masterclass and a paper-making workshop, while its shuttle bus will drop you in the centre of Florence at Piazza della Repubblica (so much easier than attempting Fiesole’s narrow, winding roads yourself). Wellness devotees are also looked after, with three treatment rooms including a double suite at Italy’s first Guerlain spa, and, up in the woods, an Energy Chapel, Sungazing Lounge and yoga deck designed by super-cool Milanese lifestyle brand La DoubleJ. Villa San Michele’s swimming pool. Letizia Cigliutti The verdict The celebration of Italian craftsmanship and the level of thoughtful detail at this historic Franciscan convent, combined with the sublime peace of its gardens, make a stay here unforgettable. Essentials

World.title: I’m a breastfeeding mum. How much should my workplace cater to me?
World.content:
LifestyleLife & relationshipsGot a Minute? I’m a breastfeeding mum. How much should my workplace cater to me? Kirstin Ferguson August 5, 2026 — 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Each week Dr Kirstin Ferguson tackles questions about workplace, career and leadership in her advice column Got a Minute? This week: a missing office after maternity leave, bogus corporate values and bring forced to take leave. The best employers welcome people back from maternity and paternity leave. Dionne Gain I’m on maternity leave, returning to work in two months. While I’ve been away, my private office has been reassigned (I now need to hot-desk) and I’ve been told I’ll need to work from a different building two days a week. Before going on leave, my employer and I agreed I could use my office to express milk when I returned, but that office is no longer mine. HR is trying to find an alternative solution but nothing is confirmed, and the options suggested so far include booking a boardroom some distance away, or using a parents’ room in an entirely different building. These feel impractical for someone who needs to express multiple times a day. Is any of this reasonable? Just because you took parental leave does not mean you should be expected to accept reduced working conditions. The best employers welcome people back from maternity and paternity leave, rather than making them feel like an imposition.



Related Article Got a Minute? My holiday was ruined by a redundancy threat. I stayed, but I’m still mad Your employer has specific legal obligations regarding breastfeeding, which is a protected ground of discrimination. The failure to provide adequate facilities may be a breach of work health and safety laws. You should request a private room with a comfortable chair, a fridge where you can store breast milk and somewhere to store your breast pump. It is difficult to see how booking out the boardroom, for example, would meet those requirements. Rather than debating the loss of your office itself, keep the discussion focused on outcomes. Explain why the proposed alternatives won’t work in practice and ask HR to work with you on a solution that is private, close and consistently available. If that doesn’t happen, you might like to seek advice from the Australian Human Rights Commission about your rights.



I work in an investment bank that has a set of values, including a “speak up” culture. However, the reality is the opposite. When issues – with evidence – were raised about a senior female executive of undermining behaviour and bullying, they were shut down by HR. This female executive has had many complaints about her behaviour; however, she continues to behave poorly, lies and manipulates her boss. Our team has suffered much turnover due to her inappropriate behaviour. How would you approach this situation? It is easy to list a bunch of values and stick them on a wall. It is much harder to actually live them. In any organisation, if values are not being lived “from the top”, the chances are the values are unlikely to be lived at all. If complaints about this woman have been repeatedly ignored despite evidence, the issue is no longer one difficult executive but a leadership culture that tolerates the behaviour. That doesn’t mean you should stop raising concerns, but be strategic. Keep records, stick to facts rather than opinions, and use whatever formal reporting channels are available. If nothing changes, consider whether you think things will ever really change. If the answer is no, sometimes the only thing you can do is send a message by taking your talents and loyalty somewhere else. My workplace has a lot of long-term staff who are constantly being pushed to take their long service leave. I understand companies do not want the high liabilities on their balance sheet, but employees feel like they are being forced to take leave when they do not want to. Are there any laws around this? Can a company legally force you to take it?



Related Article Got a Minute? My bad date is threatening to go to my employer. How can I stop her? The first thing employers need to remember is that long service leave is an entitlement, not just some sort of balance sheet problem to be dealt with. There is a big difference between encouraging someone to take their long service leave, and forcing someone to take it (the “use it or lose it” idea). While employers can sometimes direct employees to take long service leave, the rules vary between states and territories and will often depend on the circumstances. If your employer is forcing people to take leave, you can ask what policy or legal basis they’re relying on. You can check the specific long service leave rules that apply where you work by seeking advice from your union, HR or the Fair Work Ombudsman. To submit a question about work, careers or leadership, visit kirstinferguson.com/ask. You will not be asked to provide your name or any identifying information. Letters may be edited. World.title: Older Kiwis choosing between 'starving or heating' as price increases bite
World.content:
Age Concern’s Greta Bond discusses energy affordability Morning Report Download MP3 5m

An advocate for older people says recent cold temperatures combined with the cost of power and other goods have produced a crisis point, with many people forced to choose between food and heating.

Age Concern Canterbury chief executive Greta Bond told Morning Report older people on fixed incomes were having to make real choices every day about whether they will be warm or fed.

"Every week we're encountering people who are really struggling. Renters are in a particularly precarious position because they may be spending 60 or 70 percent of their pension on rent.

"It's actually a real crisis for people. I don't think people really understand or like to think that we have older people who are actively living in poverty in our country," Bond said.

Many people were resorting to spending most of their day in bed with negative consequences.

"They might get up for a little bit in the middle of the day when it's the most warm, probably not at all this week. They might just wake up in the morning, get themselves a cup of tea or something, and then just stay in bed the whole day.

"That's so bad for them in terms of their health, their physical health, their mental health, their social connection, but definitely staying in a really constricted life because they can't go out. And they might not even leave their bedroom."

While the increased costs hit those renting hard, Bond said retired home owners were also vulnerable to price rises for different reasons.

"While you have the security of tenure, you're your own landlord, so you may not have a healthy home in terms of the insulation, and maintenance may be difficult. So that home may be even colder than the rental," she said.

"As a society, we need to think about our older people and what we are prioritising.

"We aren't a country, I think, who would like to think of the fact that we've got old people who are either starving or freezing in their own homes. And, at a government level, I'd like to see more attention to that. But also individually, we can look out for our older neighbours as well," she said.

The Winter Energy Payment was welcome but it was not enough.

World.title: Veteran radio broadcaster hangs up the mic, aged 93
World.content:
A 93-year-old veteran of community radio broadcasting is hanging up his microphone after 25 years on air.

Ray Woodley has presented an assortment of music programmes in Palmerston North and he has just recorded the 700th - and last - episode of his latest show Musical Confection.

A builder by trade, Woodley only began broadcasting after he retired, but he says he has loved every minute of it.

RNZ sat in with Woodley for some of his final recording, which began: "Greetings everybody for this programme, Musical Confection, programme number 700 - how did I ever get to here?

"They've given me an hour today, so I'm going to play lots of tracks I have liked over the years - whether anybody else did, I don't know."

Ray Woodley has broadcast on community radio in Palmerston North for 25 years. RNZ / Jimmy Ellingham

Woodley has presented Musical Confection since 2011. It mainly focused on big band classics and jazz standards.

There were many other programmes in the decade before that too on the airwaves of Manawatū People's Radio - one of 12 community stations throughout New Zealand - as well as stints as an announcer and even board chairman.

"I can still remember driving my car up Rangitīkei Street for the first time, nervous as billy-o, and never thinking I'd get to 700 programmes, of this one," he said of his radio debut.

Woodley showed some emotion as he unpacked CDs neatly stacked in his briefcase and cast a last final eye over his programme's runlist.

"I've got mixed feelings about today, but that's what happens in life - parts of your life come to an end."

The end of an era did not go unmarked - a portrait of Woodley was unveiled on the radio station wall. It was drawn by radio station content co-ordinator Hugh Dingwall's daughter Leilani.

A likeness of Ray Woodley now hangs on the Manawatū People's Radio wall. RNZ / Jimmy Ellingham

And as Woodley took a break from recording his extended farewell, there was time for a few stories over a glass of alcohol-free bubbles, including the time he was on air and a woman phoned in with a request.

She wanted to hear a song she insisted was well known, Share Your Banana With Me.

Woodley said he was stumped, so consulted the then-station manager, who eventually worked out the caller meant Kiwi classic, Sir John Rowles' Cheryl Moana Marie, which Woodley played on air. The woman rang back, thankful to learn the song's real name.

Woodley said the nerves of his early days were gone, although he admitted he was not as confident as he once was.

But he was grateful the small team at Manawatū People's Radio looked after him.

Dingwall said Woodley was full of surprises, and was a generous man who would regularly bring in fresh produce from his garden.

"He's definitely going to be missed," Dingwall said.

"Because he lives at Olive Tree, at a rest home, he's in direct contact with a lot of people who are his listeners, in a way that's quite unusual for our shows.

"He'll get people knocking on his door saying, That was a good one you did, Ray."

Ray Woodley was at time emotional as he began his final recording, aged 93. RNZ / Jimmy Ellingham

Woodley was a stalwart of the Manawatū music scene, Dingwall said.

"In many ways he's kind of a last window into a world of music that doesn't exist any more. He had an early career as an itinerant piano player.

"There was a period of time where every building had a piano, so if you were having a party you hired a guy to come and play it, and in Manawatū that guy was Ray. He had to know every popular song off the top of his head."

Woodley is also a banjo player and, around his day job, managed bands.

He will now have a gap in his weekly schedule, which he said he would probably fill with more lunches and more piano playing at the rest home.

"It does seem a bit strange. I'll probably find for a couple of weeks I might think, hello, what should I be doing today?

"It's my 25th year and 700 programmes - it's probably a good time to call it off."

World.title: BNZ increases home loan rates
World.content:
Do I have to buy that extended warranty? No Stupid Questions with Susan Edmunds Download MP3 12m

BNZ has become the latest bank to put up its home loan rates.

It is increasing its standard one-year rate by 20 basis points to 4.99 percent.

The 18-month rate also increases by the same margin, to 5.29 percent.

Two- and three-year rates will lift by 16 basis points and four-year rates by six, all to 5.45 percent.

It follows ANZ, which said increases were due to rising wholesale rates.

Infometrics chief forecaster Gareth Kiernan said financial markets had priced in the official cash rate getting to 3 percent or slightly above by the end of this year and 3.5 percent by the middle of next year.

"That's in line with our forecast, pretty much all of what I expected is already priced into rates. You might get another 10 basis points, maybe slightly more on the one-year rate before the end of the year but I don't see a great deal of pressure on the one-year rates past that.

"Even through 2027 as the expected rate increases become reality you might get a bit more but I'm talking about a one-year rate at maybe 5.4 percent and the two-year at 5.7 percent. It's not huge, assuming the world behaves itself, there's not massive amounts of lift left."

He said it was unlikely that home loan rates would get into the 6 percent range again.

World.title: Should customers pay less when they use a self-checkout?
World.content:
Do I have to buy that extended warranty? No Stupid Questions with Susan Edmunds Download MP3 12m

Who is really saving money when supermarket shoppers check out and bag their own groceries?

That is a question New York lawmakers have reportedly been pondering.

State representative Nikki Lucas has introduced a bill that would require retail businesses selling food in the state to offer a 10 percent discount to those who used the self-checkout lane.

"Retail businesses increasingly rely on self-checkout systems to reduce staffing and operational costs by shifting responsibilities traditionally performed by employees onto consumers," she wrote.

Who really benefits from self checkout machines? Morning Report Download MP3 3m

"Since customers are effectively completing portions of the checkout labor themselves without compensation, providing a mandatory discount helps ensure fairness, acknowledges consumer participation in store operations, and allows the public to share in the financial savings created by self-service technology."

Consumer NZ head of advocacy Gemma Rasmussen said her organisation thought there was validity to the argument in New Zealand, too.

"If you're serving yourself then ultimately the supermarket is saving money through less staff resourcing, and those savings are not currently being passed on to shoppers.

"Pak'n Save advertises themselves as a cheaper place to shop given you pack your bags yourself. It seems many businesses are moving towards fewer staff and more technological assistance, for example there are now fewer bank branches across New Zealand, and more chatbots instead of call centre representatives across a number of major businesses. Ultimately this provides a cost saving for the business, not the consumer."

She said concern about the price of food and groceries was still the number one financial worry for most people.

"When we started tracking financial concerns in 2022, food pricing was the 8th highest concern. Lowering prices for shoppers who choose to self-serve would be one way to alleviate some of these cost pressures, however we're dubious the supermarkets would introduce such a discount."

University of Auckland marketing expert Professor Michael Lee said it made sense from a fairness point-of-view.

"The supermarkets are saving ongoing cost of labour by automating that portion of their operations. Therefore, why not to pass on the savings to their loyal customers?"

He said in a market like New Zealand, it was unlikely that retailers would make the choice to offer a discount, unless they were compelled to.

"Unless one of the retailers, or a new entrant, decided to take this approach, there would little incentive for either to do so, meaning that the two main retailers would continue to use such cost savings to extend their profit margin."

Foodstuffs said self-checkouts were one of a number of ways customers could choose to shop, alongside traditional staffed checkouts.

"Many customers value the convenience, speed and flexibility that self-service offers, particularly when buying a small number of items. We continue to invest in both self-service and staffed checkouts so customers can choose the option that best suits their needs. Team members are always available to assist customers using self-checkouts and to operate staffed lanes. Our focus is on giving customers choice and making shopping as easy and convenient as possible."

Woolworths said in a statement it thought customers found it convenient to have options.

World.title: Unemployment expected to push up to near 11-year high, economists warn
World.content:
Unemployment expected to edge higher to around 5.5 percent - data due 5 August, 10.45 am

Economic activity slowed by US-Iran war, firms not hiring, but more people in workforce

Labour market recovery not until next year

Wage growth to remain subdued at 2 percent, lagging inflation

Data not likely to deter RBNZ from further cash rate rises

Unemployment is set to push up to a near 11-year high with too many people and a weak supply of jobs.

Major bank economists expect the unemployment rate to inch up to 5.4 or 5.5 percent for the three months ended June, from the 5.3 percent rate in March.

Westpac senior economist Michael Gordon said employment growth is subdued.

"The jobs market has held its ground through the Middle East conflict, but it hasn't gathered the momentum that we would have otherwise hoped to see.

"Employment has been gradually picking up again in recent months, but not quickly enough to keep up with population growth."

Expectations are that a few thousand jobs may have been created during the quarter.

ANZ senior economist Miles Workman said businesses had not been firing staff to any extent, but weak economic activity meant there was little hiring either.

"Overall, the Q2 data are expected to paint a relatively soft picture of the labour market, with firms having pressed the pause button in response to the oil price shock and heightened global uncertainty."

He said he would be looking for clues on the underlying state of the labour market, such as the number of hours worked.

"Firms typically reduce available hours during a downturn before resorting to layoffs, particularly when they expect any weakness to be temporary."

Labour market numbers can be a statistical lottery, with the unemployment rate influenced by the size of the workforce, how many are participating, are doing training, have stopped looking for work, irrespective of how many jobs may have been created.

Other labour market indicators have painted a generally gloomy picture.

The Institute of Economic Research's June quarterly survey (QSBO) showed weak demand for staff, while the Westpac-McDermott Miller Employment Confidence index plunged to its lowest reading since its inception.

Peak unemployment?

An economic cliché is that the labour market is "a lagging indicator" - it's the last part of the economy to fall in a downturn and the last to rebound in the recovery.

ASB acting chief economist Kim Mundy was crossing fingers that the latest number is likely be peak unemployment, volatility aside.

"Hopefully this is as high as unemployment is going to go ... should things happen as we expect them to we expect the economy to generate more momentum as we go into the end of this year and entrench a labour market recovery in 2027."

Wages are expected to have grown around 2 percent over the past year, which would satisfy the Reserve Bank (RBNZ) that there is little risk in it adding to inflation pressures driven to a two year high of 4.1 percent by the US-Iran war.

The RBNZ no longer has a specific instruction to help the labour market and maximise employment, but nonetheless always casts an eye over labour market health.

ANZ's Workman said labour market weakness was one factor helping to contain inflation pressures.

World.title: Father who thought parking fine text was a scam angry at Ministry of Justice warnings
World.content:
An Auckland father of three is angry the Ministry of Justice threatened his pregnant wife with arrest over a parking fine.

Matt Ward says they dismissed a text from the ministry in March, thinking it was a scam because it contained a payment link, only to receive the threat of arrest in a follow-up text last month.

"It's gone... zero to a hundred with a couple of text messages saying we're going to arrest you, which is just ridiculous," he told RNZ.

Auckland Transport (AT) said it mailed the infringement notice but Ward said they never received it - their neighbourhood has no mail delivery.

AT said it wished it had other options beyond mail.

"We would be in favour of updates to NZTA's system so emails or phone numbers can be included with vehicle registration details."

The Ministry of Justice Ministry said the texts it sent Ward were legitimate. It was still putting a payment link in texts in March, but dropped them in April.

"Since this text was received [by Ward], links have been removed from text messages to help the public differentiate between legitimate and scam texts," said the ministry.

Ward said the whole thing was bizarre and heavy-handed, with a system that appeared to be broken.

They complained last month and have been told the infringement had been removed from the courts.

'So many ads and warnings about links'

Ward said there was no ticket on the windscreen of his wife's car when he got back after parking it in central Auckland in September.

Parking wardens still leave tickets, but the council's number-plate-identifying patrol cars do not. AT sends out letters.

Six months later, on 17 March, his wife - who did not want to be identified - received a text saying a fine was due in seven days.

It gave an 0800 number and said "or click here to pay online" with a link, but they were suspicious.

"There's so many ads and warnings out there about links, and not clicking on links," said Ward.

She received a second text from a district court deputy registrar on 6 July saying: "I have noticed that you have not kept your arrangement to pay your fines. I am now considering issuing a warrant to arrest."

His wife was three days away from having a baby when she got the text.

"It came as a massive shock," said Ward.

"Surely the threat of arrest is more of a phone-call conversation rather than sending a casual text message."

He defended not calling the ministry to query the text in March

"Why would the Ministry of Justice be getting in touch when you hadn't even heard from Auckland Transport or a debt collection agency?"

Ward searched online in July and found a ministry web page stating it did not put links in texts.

The fine was sitting at $208 when they got the second text.

Ward said he then called the ministry only to be told there was a fine. He has disputed it and laid a complaint.

"The systems are a little bit broken if this is what happens," he said.

'Paper-based processes'

Multiple agencies - including NZTA and police - have warned that texts with payment links are not from them and are a scam.

A justice ministry online post from 24 March listed three things a legitimate text will have - but a payment link is not one of them. But it told RNZ: "Fines-related text messages included links until 30 March 2026."

It said in a statement it would keep on reviewing and updating its information to "reflect the evolving environment".

"The ministry is aware that scam text messages continue to circulate from time to time," it said.

"We continue to monitor the situation and provide the public with information to help them identify genuine contact for the court."

Auckland Transport said the system could be better.

"The letter was sent to the person and address that the vehicle is registered to in the NZTA database. This is the only way we are able to correspond, based on NZTA's paper-based processes.

"We would be in favour of updates to this system so emails or phone numbers can be included with vehicle registration details and letters such as this are not discarded when they are delivered addressed to a different person."

Ward said they had a mailing address separate from their physical address, but did not receive an infringement letter there.

World.title: NRLW great Ali Brigginshaw gets three-match ban
World.content:
Brisbane Broncos skipper Ali Brigginshaw has been handed a three-week ban for a dangerous tackle and will miss a major chunk of the rest of the NRLW home-and-away season.

Brigginshaw was sent straight to the judiciary for her tackle on Canterbury's Tayla Preston during Magic Round at Wagga Wagga.

The Broncos lead the competition with a 5-0 record, but Brigginshaw will now be unavailable until round 9, three games before the finals series.

As Preston ran the ball away from her goal line, Brigginshaw advanced and grabbed the Bulldogs player, then spun her around before lifting her up and bringing her down on her head.

Preston avoided serious injury and Brigginshaw was charged with a grade 3 dangerous throw.

Brigginshaw thanked the judiciary panel for considering her case and reiterated her remorse for the incident.

"I meant absolutely no malice in making the tackle, I apologised to Tayla post-match and have been in contact with her again since, she was accepting of my apology on both occasions," she said.

"I'm looking forward to getting back on the field in a few weeks and finishing my playing career on a positive note."

The 36-year-old, who is playing her final season of NRLW before retirement, has not missed a Broncos game since the competition's inception in 2018.

Sydney Roosters forward Aliyah Nasio was the last NRLW player to be referred directly to the judiciary following a brawl at the conclusion of last year's grand final, when she struck Brisbane's Julia Robinson.

Nasio was banned for four matches after being hit with a grade 3 striking charge.

In 2023, Parramatta's Kennedy Cherrington was also banned for four weeks after being charged with a grade 3 dangerous throw.

World.title: Clarkson happy with handshake to extend contract as North set to miss finals
World.content:
North Melbourne coach Alastair Clarkson is unfazed going into the final year of his contract, saying he just needs a "handshake".

As Clarkson comes towards the end of his fourth season in charge, North will spend a 10th-straight year without experiencing finals action.

Speculation has started to mount that Kangaroos hierarchy might consider letting Clarkson go at the end of his current five-year deal, signed in late 2022 in what was a massive coup for the club.

Although North have improved this year, they are yet to beat a team above them on the ladder and will fall short of a wildcard berth.

AFL round 21 Saturday live updates Josh Fraser's bid to become Carlton's next full-time coach receives a massive boost as the Blues record a thumping win over the Brisbane Lions.

"Old school" Clarkson will not be pushing for a contract extension beyond 2027 this off-season and is happy to wait it out.

"All I require is a handshake and a wink and a nod, and that'll do me," the four-time Hawthorn premiership coach said on Tuesday.

"We'll work our way through whatever we need to do.

"I'm really here to serve the footy club … it's not just me, but those that are in leadership positions at the club have done a really good job stabilising the footy club.

"We're really keen to progress and get ourselves up the ladder, but all we do know is that that's done best when you've got stability."

Clarkson drew on examples of Brisbane Lions, Fremantle and Adelaide of clubs who were patient with their coaches and find themselves in powerful positions on the field.

"I've been in the caper for a long time, so that's a bit of water off the duck's (back)," he said of speculation about his future.

"The best examples are the reigning premiers (Brisbane) who took a while to get going and then Adelaide with 'Nicksy' (Matthew Nicks) and Fremantle with Justin Longmuir.

"The governance and administration of the club just sticking to the path and sticking to the course, and we're going to be no different."

Clarkson's record at North is 19-1-59, a far cry from his glory years with the Hawks.

The Kangaroos face a challenging run home, starting with the Western Bulldogs at Docklands on Thursday night.

They have long losing streaks against the Bulldogs, and their final two opponents, Geelong and Sydney.

ABC Sport Daily podcast ABC Sport Daily is your daily sports conversation. We dive into the biggest story of the day and get you up to speed with everything else that's making headlines.

Clarkson bristled when asked how important it would be to beat one of those teams to finish off this season.

"You're just searching, searching for a headline," he said.

"Teams that have been in the bottom four or five on the ladder haven't beaten the top teams very often in the last five or six years.

"That's the reason why they've been in that position on the ladder."

AAP

World.title: Clubs stand firm after AFL's controversial finals memo
World.content:
The AFL's warning to clubs about resting players before the newly introduced wildcard round has not gone down well with coaches.

Clubs have been threatened with sanctions if they decide to make mass changes for their games in round 24.

"While legitimate player management of player fatigue or injuries is permitted, the AFL will scrutinise club team selection decisions in the lead-up to AFL finals," AFL football boss Greg Swann wrote in a memo to clubs on Monday.

The AFL has had a pre-finals bye since 2016, allowing the top-eight teams a week off before the last month of the season.

But with the finals system effectively becoming a top-10 due to the wildcard weekend, not every club will be afforded that luxury should they qualify.

Teams ranked seventh to 10th at the end of the home-and-away season will have to back up and play the following week.

The top-six will all rest before preparing for respective qualifying and elimination finals, starting on September 3.

The Western Bulldogs are almost certain to finish in the wildcard bracket, creating a dilemma for coach Luke Beveridge.

"The main consideration for the teams who might be certainties to play a wildcard game going into that round is the fact that the six teams above the seventh have all got a week off," Beveridge told Fox Footy.

ABC Sport Daily podcast ABC Sport Daily is your daily sports conversation. We dive into the biggest story of the day and get you up to speed with everything else that's making headlines.

"I'm sure within the ranks of the teams that are certainties, you're processing who needs a week off.

"I'd question how the AFL could question a club, because you're questioning the medical department from a club as well, if that happens."

Steven King, in his rookie season as Melbourne coach, was also left perplexed by the AFL's directive.

"I'm the coach of the Melbourne footy club," he told Fox Footy.

"I'll make any decision that's best for our football club and best for the management of our players."

The Dockers made a string of changes for the last home-and-away round in 2013, then travelled to Geelong and beat the Cats in finals. (Getty Images: Michael Dodge)

Fremantle famously made 10 changes for their final home-and-away game in 2013, leading to them being thrashed by struggling St Kilda.

The following week, the Dockers pulled off a historic qualifying-final win in Geelong over the highly fancied Cats.

In 2015, North Melbourne rested nine players ahead of a finals campaign when they lost against Richmond.

The move paid off for the Kangaroos, who turned the tables on the Tigers in an elimination final and also won a semi-final in Sydney.

Former North Melbourne coach Brad Scott rested nine players in the final round of the 2015 season, while Ross Lyon made 10 changes in the final round of the 2013 season when he was in charge of Fremantle.

AAP

World.title: Aussie swimmer out of leadership group after reported drinking session
World.content:
Australian swimmer Isaac Cooper has stepped down from the Dolphins's leadership group after a drinking session at the Commonwealth Games.

Cooper was reported to be out drinking when he was expected to be supporting teammates at Glasgow's Tollcross International Swimming Centre last Wednesday night.

Cooper was also seen drinking at the Australian team hotel during that day, the report said.

"Isaac did not attend the final night of the swimming competition or final team meeting in Glasgow, which is in conflict with team expectations," a Swimming Australia statement said.

What the Commonwealth Games mean is up to you Australian chef de mission and eight-time Olympic medallist Petria Thomas cried as she spoke about the importance of the Commonwealth Games to her, so it doesn't really matter if it felt too easy for Australia at times.

"Isaac has since voluntarily stood down from the team's athlete leadership group."

Cooper was scheduled to race the 100m backstroke final that night but withdrew from the event after qualifying eighth-fastest.

Swimmers were expected to support teammates at the Glasgow Games when not racing, while Cooper also missed the team meeting that night.

The 22-year-old won gold at the Glasgow Games as a member of the 4x100m medley team after swimming in the heats.

He also finished sixth in the 50m backstroke final, an event he won a silver medal at the 2024 world championships.

Cooper will next compete at the Pan Pacific championships in the United States starting August 12.

AAP

World.title: Blues announce King as new Origin coach after Daley steps down
World.content:
Former NSW State of Origin player Matt King has been named the new head coach of the Blues.

King was announced as the new coach on Tuesday after predecessor Laurie Daley stepped down from the role on Monday.

Blues pay tribute to 'hero' Daley as he stands down as coach The NSWRL pays tribute to Blues "hero" Laurie Daley as the coach stands down from his role after this year's series win over Queensland.

King played nine times for the Blues from 2005-2007, and over 200 first grade matches for Melbourne, South Sydney and Warrington across the NRL and Super League in England.

"I'm very clear on what it looks like to be the head coach of NSW," King said.

"I have a true understanding of what it means to lead this great state of ours and I can't wait for that opportunity.

"The one true rugby league love of my life has been the NSW Blues. To know now that I have the opportunity to guide the team moving forward, to lead the program over the next little period, means the absolute world to me."

The 45-year-old has been a long-time assistant coach under Trent Robinson at the Sydney Roosters, and has been part of the Blues' coaching staff since 2024.

Daley stepped down as Blues coach on Monday after guiding NSW to a series win this year.

The Blues sealed the series with a 30-12 triumph in the decider at Lang Park, just the fourth time NSW has won a deciding Game III in Brisbane.

Daley slams 'hidden agendas' after NSW Origin win Laurie Daley has the last laugh over critics who hounded him ahead of the State of Origin decider at Lang Park.

"I've always considered it an absolute honour and privilege to be involved with the NSW Blues State of Origin team, whether that was as a player or a coach, and I've always been ready to answer the call for my state whenever they needed me," Daley said in a statement on Monday.

"We faced plenty of challenges in the 2026 series and I'm proud of the way the players banded together to overcome them and save their best performance for Game Three in Brisbane to secure a memorable series win.

"I thank the fans for their passion and their support, and I can't think of a better way to move on with the Shield back where it belongs in NSW."

World.title: Haugset goes it alone to claim Tour de France Femmes third stage
World.content:
Sigrid Haugset has set off on a long solo run and kept going to the finish to win the third stage of the Women's Tour de France and claim the yellow jersey.

The Norwegian rider made her break with more than half of the tough 156.5-kilometre route between Geneva and Poligny to go.

The stage featured four categorised climbs and Haugset made her move with 85 kilometres left, at the foot of the category two Col de la Savine.

Haugset was also first across the last listed climb of the day, the category four Côte de Chaux-Champagny, followed by Lotte Kopecky about 30 seconds behind, and a nine-rider group more than two minutes adrift.

Previous yellow jersey holder Lorena Wiebes, who won the first two stages, was 13 minutes behind with the main bunch at the time. She ultimately finished more than 20 minutes adrift of Haugset and dropped to 67th in the general classification.

It was a battle between two riders going into the last 10 kilometres. Kopecky had cut Haugset's lead to 15 seconds and the Belgian rider could just about see her rival ahead.

But Haugset, sensing the danger, stood on her pedals to stay ahead and managed to increase her lead again, finishing 1:24 ahead of Kopecky.

Haugset leads the general classification by 2:02 from Kimberley Le Court of Mauritius, with 2023 Tour champion Demi Vollering third, a further four seconds behind.

This edition of the race, the fifth of the Women's Tour, covers 1,175 kilometres over nine days.

World.title: Infantino could face UEFA lawsuit as he scrambles for FIFA presidency support
World.content:
European football body UEFA has threatened FIFA with legal action over Gianni Infantino's failed plan to sell a stake in future World Cup profits to private investors, and says potential evidence should not be destroyed.

Mr Infantino on Saturday dropped a secretive proposal to raise $US4.2 billion ($6 billion) from investors, including the New York investment firm of Joshua Kushner, days after media reports revealed it, provoking a global furore.

UEFA led the backlash and its 55 member federations met to agree to boycott all FIFA events and competitions while the proposal was active.

Now UEFA's lawyers have informed FIFA that the European body is "actively considering legal action, arbitration, and/or regulatory complaints … arising out of and in connection with the FFE (FIFA Forward Enterprise) plan proposed by FIFA and all related matters".

The letter named 18 FIFA executives who it said should retain data, documents and electronic messages as potential evidence. They include Mr Infantino, Zurich-based chief finance officer Thomas Peyer and Arsène Wenger, the coaching great who is FIFA's head of global football development.

Football bodies launch stunning Infantino rebuke Two of football's major bodies launch stinging rebukes of FIFA boss Gianni Infantino after his failed privatisation ploy.

"UEFA puts you on formal notice that any destruction, deletion, alteration, concealment, or loss of relevant materials following receipt of this notice — or following any earlier date on which you were, or reasonably should have been, aware that proceedings were anticipated — may constitute spoliation of evidence," the letter said.

Meanwhile, the Swedish football federation confirmed that UEFA is actively looking "to come up with an alternative candidate" as FIFA president. The next election is scheduled in March.

On Saturday, UEFA signalled it wants to end Mr Infantino's decade-long presidency, saying he had lost the confidence of world football and that "no option should be off the table".

Hours earlier, Mr Infantino had withdrawn the divisive proposal that offered FIFA's 211 member federations one-off payments of $20 million each with a mid-September deadline to accept.

The FFE spin-off valued by FIFA at $20 billion would have taken control of the football body's money-making commercial and tournament operations through at least 2038. It promised to more than double development money over that time for the 211 members who already effectively own the Zurich-based not-for-profit governing body.

It was the project of just one man, FIFA's chief operating officer Kevin Lamour said in a stinging statement that said staff felt deceived by their boss Mr Infantino.

FIFA COO Kevin Lamour has made clear his opposition to Gianni Infantino's plan. (Getty Images: Joosep Martinson)

Legal proceedings are "reasonably anticipated," UEFA's lawyer Andrew J Levander wrote, citing the belief of football stakeholders that the plan was "fundamentally incompatible with the proper governance of football".

UEFA has been outspoken against its former employee Mr Infantino, while the Asian Football Confederation and CONCACAF also made strong statements opposing Mr Infantino's plan.

Mr Infantino has most support from his traditional base in Africa, while South America's CONMEBOL is relying on him to expand the 2030 World Cup to 64 teams from 48. That would give more hosting games to Argentina, Uruguay and Paraguay, the home country of CONMEBOL president Alejandro Dominguez.

Gianni Infantino is reportedly seeking support from Donald Trump in his FIFA presidency battle. (Reuters: Dylan Martinez)

Mr Infantino's path to stabilising the presidency he has held for more than 10 years was unclear. A report yesterday claimed he was seeking support from the administration of his close ally US President Donald Trump, possibly in a call with Secretary of State Marco Rubio.

"There are no plans for @SecRubio to speak with Mr Infantino and there is no call this morning," Dylan Johnson, assistant secretary of state for global public affairs, posted on social media.

The 56-year-old FIFA leader left New York after the World Cup final two weeks ago seemingly a lock to be re-elected unopposed next March for a fourth and final term in office through 2031.

FIFA briefed at the World Cup that Mr Infantino had pledged letters of support from about 200 of the 211 member federations.

Those letters are now likely being withdrawn across Europe, with the Wales federation the first to announce its reversal.

The candidate deadline is November 18 for an election four months later in Morocco.
